subsubtopic: NOMINATION OF SENATORS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise concerning the disgraceful, Machiavellian manoeuvring of politics and Parliament crassly committed yesterday by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) through the elevation of the Senate of his canoeing pal from Spadina in an attempt to prepare a path to this House for Toronto's little cherub, James Coutts, first of the flunkies to precede the Prime Minister's own delayed departure. 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling):
That this House condemns the shameless playing with power for political purposes by the Prime Minister, his abusive actions of snickering at the Senate while filling it with friends, flunkies and worn-out sacred cows of the Liberal party and making a mockery of our political system for his own autocratic ends and, finally, requests the Prime Minister to advise us immediately when the next exodus is to be made by Michael Pitfield to the position of Undersecretary of State for External Affairs.

speechtext:

Considering that the purpose of government policies and agencies is theoretically to assist and not impair Canadians in pursuit of legitimate goals; considering that many small business enterprises, already imperilled by this government's high interest rate policy, are further threatened by the unhappy situation in the government-operated Post Office; and considering that many small business enterprises such as Beaven's Custom Cannery in Summerland, British Columbia, are seasonal enterprises and that any disruption in normal mail communication with customers at this time threatens the entire annual production and profitability, without which the business must fail; I move, seconded by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling):

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I too rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Given that the responsibility to provide adequate financial and human resources to maintain the integrity of Canada's air traffic control system lies with the federal government, and since air traffic control services at the Calgary International Airport will be curtailed between the hours of 12 midnight and 6 a.m. effective July 4 because of insufficient numbers of air traffic controllers, thereby seriously impairing the ability to provide positive separation between aircraft and aircraft and surface vehicles, as well as raising serious questions of legal liability, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington):
That the minister take immediate steps to maintain full 24-hour air traffic control services at Calgary International and that emergency steps be taken to fill the 22 vacant ATC positions in Vancouver, 12 in Calgary, 15 in Edmonton, 58 in Toronto, 50 in Montreal, and 20 in Gander, plus an additional 75 controllers in other points in Canada.

subsubtopic: LEVEL OF FOREIGN RESERVES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Finance and touches, of course, on the news this morning that our foreign reserves have fallen to the lowest level in ten years. Would the minister indicate to the House why that has occurred and is it in fact government policy to run with such slim reserves backing our dollar? In short, what level do ministers intend to maintain? They are down to almost S3 billion now; is that the level they hope to maintain, or are they content to see reserves slip away to the $2 billion, or $1 billion level, or even less?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: LEVEL OF FOREIGN RESERVES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I must say I am surprised at the hon. member suggesting the reserves might be at a low level. I regard them as being in a very healthy condition, particularly when one looks at the gold holdings in the amount of $842 million at book value. If they were shown at market value it would increase the reserves to an extraordinary high level.

Madam Speaker, as I indicated, the reserves are at an historically low level, certainly over the last ten years. In relation to our trade they are at a very, very low percentage of our total activity.
Let me put my second question touching on this matter to the Minister of Finance. Bill Jarvis, an economist with Infor-metrica, stated that investor uncertainty over Canadian policies, especially in energy, is continuing to put our dollar under pressure and that a solution to the energy dispute between Ottawa and Alberta would go a long way toward strengthening the dollar and the reserves. If the government could settle the energy question, is it not true that it would relieve the outgo of Canadian dollars considerably, an outgo on petroleum

July 3, 1981

products alone which was up 36 per cent in May of this year compared with May, 1980, due largely to the almost ludicrous position taken by the federal government of being willing to buy from a foreigner but not from our provinces such as British Columbia or Alberta?
Hon Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance): Madam Speaker, I do not want to be contentious with the hon. member about foreign exchange reserves, but I would suggest that when he compares the reserves of ten years ago he might look at the comparative prices for gold and translate into current market value the reserves of gold which we hold at the present time. But that is by way of suggesting that the hon. member reconsider his point.
With respect to the energy settlement, it is as clear to me, as it is to others, that there would be a number of benefits flowing from an energy settlement including, we would hope, the end of production cutbacks which are putting additional strain on our balance of payments. That in itself would improve the situation.
Furthermore, an energy settlement would remove an uncertainty which presently exists, and that would be helpful. It is for these reasons that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and his counterpart in Alberta have been working very constructively in their last meetings in order to reach an energy settlement.

Madam Speaker, again my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. You will recall that in answer to a question yesterday dealing with high interest rates in this country, higher than any of the other six main industrialized nations, the minister came back with the odd comment that he had found in Germany that interest rates on a real basis were also at the highest level they had ever been in Germany. We must be encouraged that the minister has started to take a look at the economy of Germany. Has he also noticed that since 1973 Germany has run with an inflation level approximately half our inflation level, and an unemployment level approximately half the unemployment level of this country? Does he feel he could perhaps learn from what the Germans have been doing in running their economy, and run a better economy here with lower interest rates and certainly lower inflation?
If the hon. member put some stock in comparing performances among industrialized countries, he ought to be impressed by the fact that job creation in Canada on a year-to-year basis has been the highest of any industrialized country in the world, including Germany. That, to me, is a rather important fact which he is overlooking.
Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ACTION TO STIMULATE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the minister responsible for housing who will know that last year Canada had the lowest number of housing starts in years. He will also know that high mortgage interest rates have severely affected the number of housing starts this year. Builders are reluctant to enter into building programs which would alleviate the low vacancy rates in multiple unit dwellings. Last year at this time the mortgage interest rate was 13 per cent. It is now running at 18.5 per cent. What new action is the government taking to stimulate housing starts in the forthcoming months?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subsubtopic: ACTION TO STIMULATE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, what the hon. member omitted to tell us in the introduction to his question was that although last year housing starts were at an exceptionally low level, seasonally-adjusted, for example, for the month of June at 125,000, a 15-year low, in the first quarter of this year there was an equally remarkable turn-around resulting in the seasonally adjusted rate for the month of March being somewhere over 242,000 which is a five-year record high for building starts in this country.
I know that most members who watch the industry know that the ups and downs are not really desirable. They certainly do not bring stability to the industry. It is our hope that the strength of the industry which has been demonstrated is one which will continue. It is our observation that the action taken by the Minister of Finance through the reintroduction of MURBs, a provision which was thought unnecessary and was dropped by the government of the hon. member's party when it was in office, is part of the bounce-back of the industry.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ACTION TO STIMULATE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member has again drawn attention to his conclusion that Canada is running the highest interest rates of any country in the world. If he looked today at the prime rate between Canada and the United States, or compared both rates, he would find that they are about the same. If he looked at the short-term rates, commercial paper in the United States, he would find that in the last week its rates have increased to some extent and that our comparable rates have dropped.

FORECAST OF DECLINE IN HOUSING STARTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same minister. The minister made reference to the seasonally adjusted starts in the first quarter of this year. Mr. Frank Clayton, a recognized expert in the housing field, has said it is hard to believe responsible government spokespersons have actually taken this position in public. Would the minister not agree that the housing starts which took place in April and May of this year were pre-sales

which were made when interest rates were much lower than they are today, and that builders arranged those mortgages when rates were much lower than they are today? Would the minister also not agree with Mr. Clayton's statement that a sharp deterioration in housing starts is unavoidable in the coming months if interest rates continue in the 18.5 per cent bracket?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subtopic: FORECAST OF DECLINE IN HOUSING STARTS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would not join in the hon. member's pessimism about the industry. I certainly do not share the pessimistic view he takes from his selective editing of Mr. Clayton's statements. If he goes on and reads Mr. Clayton's statements he will see that he projects starts at somewhere around 180,000 for this year. That number is in line with what CMHC has projected for this year and, in my view, it is a response to the strength and the need demonstrated in the market. I really see no reason for pessimism when the need and the response to it are parallel.

subsubtopic: MINISTER'S COMMITMENTS TO IMPROVE PENSIONS FOR WOMEN
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Health and Welfare. In view of the fact that it is now a year since Parliament passed the bill which added $35 a month to the guaranteed income supplement, and in view of the fact that three months have gone by since the holding of the National Pension Conference, does the minister not agree that it is time she obtained the government's support for some of her commitments to our older people, particularly by bringing in pension improvements and adjustments for women between the ages of 60 and 65, or 55 and 65, especially those who are alone and who, as the minister knows, are in greatest need?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Begin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MINISTER'S COMMITMENTS TO IMPROVE PENSIONS FOR WOMEN
speechtext:
I know, Madam Speaker, that women in particular, and unemployed people between age 50 or 55 to the age of retirement, do face an unwritten discrimination in employment, and do have the greatest difficulties, often having to go from unemployment insurance benefits to welfare. I realize that. However, my commitment which I have given to Canadians is and has always been the same.
I have recognized that were it not for constitutional matters we would not be capable of entering that field in the future in which I will live. That is what I have always acknowledged. I have always asked Canadians to accept that the first target group and the first priority, which is the policy of this government, should be the people over 65 who still lack money in order to be, once and for all, above the poverty line. I have always added that we cannot do that in the immediate future.
Oral Questions
It will be as soon as the economy picks up. That is the commitment I have given to Canadians.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER PRESS FOR ACTION BY GOVERNMENT
REQUEST THAT MINISTER PRESS FOR ACTION BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: I wonder if the Minister of National Health and Welfare has paid attention to the statements the Minister of Finance makes day after day about the economy being strong. If there are the billions of dollars of money in this country, should the Minister of National Health and Welfare not make sure that the burden of any financial difficulty the government has is not borne by older people? Does she not believe in some redistribution and some sharing? Should she not be pressing for action now instead of claiming that we cannot improve pensions in a time of restraint?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, not only has the Minister of National Health and Welfare made the commitments to older people to which she has referred today, but she has been a very strong advocate of serious reform of our income tax laws, bearing in mind that at the present time the government hands out all kinds of subsidies to people who do not need them. speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Begin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: MINISTER'S ROLE IN ADVOCATING INCOME TAX REFORMS
speechtext: May I answer that I wish I knew the exact answer to that, in the sense that the hon. member knows very well that the preparation of the budget and the decision-making process regarding budgetary measures, and, of course, income tax changes, belong to the Minister of Finance under our British parliamentary system. subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF BACK TO WORK LEGISLATION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
INTRODUCTION OF BACK TO WORK LEGISLATION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister and relates to statements made this morning in the Montreal Gazette and on "Canada A.M.", quoting unnamed Liberal MPs and a Liberal cabinet minister to the effect that back to work legislation would be introduced to settle the postal strike before Parliament rises for the summer. In light of statements made in the House yesterday by the President of the Treasury Board that such legislation was not contemplated at this time, and the much stronger statement by the Postmaster General that the government was prepared to wait until a settlement of the strike was reached at the bargaining table, through you, Madam Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister if the government has a common policy with respect to back to work legislation. If so, what is it specifically? Do we have one policy being followed by the minister responsible for bargaining, another policy being followed by the minister responsible for the Post Office, and still another being promised and followed by certain other members of cabinet and the Liberal caucus?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF BACK TO WORK LEGISLATION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have that quote from the Montreal Gazette that the hon. member refers to, and I see no indication here, but perhaps I have not read it all, that any members of cabinet have taken a contrary view to that of-

subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF BACK TO WORK LEGISLATION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: On "Canada A.M." this morning.

subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF BACK TO WORK LEGISLATION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: I have to listen to that too.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF BACK TO WORK LEGISLATION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Believe Richard Gwynn.

subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF BACK TO WORK LEGISLATION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: You never know what they are doing to you.

speechtext:
I will tell you, Madam Speaker, that both ministers were speaking on behalf of the government yesterday and I am prepared to repeat that position which is clearly the government's position. I do not know if backbenchers have or have not expressed contrary views, and to what party they belong.
I do know that cabinet has taken the position that the President of the Treasury Board and his officials have made a very fair offer. It is an offer which would give the letter sorters something like $25,000 per year. We think that is a fair offer and we think it should be discussed. We are sorry and regretful that the union negotiators have refused to come to the table to even discuss this. We have taken the clear position that there is no intention to settle this strike by legislation. It will, and should be settled by the bargaining process.

subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF BACK TO WORK LEGISLATION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I suppose we should recognize that the Prime Minister has sent his newspaper reader to Spadina and now he is going to have to learn to read newspapers himself.

Madam Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Postmaster General. In the last 24 hours, through no fault of theirs, he has had to lay off letter carriers and truck drivers, but he took almost no action last weekend or before the strike to avert it. May I ask him how long this unfortunate strike must go on before he will assume his responsibility to ensure that his employees can get back to work and that the people of Canada can have the return of their mail service?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, the letter carriers are off duty status for the present time. That is quite understandable because there is a lack of work. In answering the question of the hon. member, I will repeat what I said yesterday, that this will end as soon as the two parties get back to the table and negotiate a settlement. We hope that will be soon.

subsubtopic: DATE OF HEARING RESPECTING SPADINA ELECTION RESULT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. In view of the announcement yesterday of the appointment to the other place of Peter Stollery, will the Prime Minister indicate to the House whether he was aware that a trial date had been set for next September 14 for the hearing of a petition under the Controverted Elections Act, the result of which might well void the election of Mr. Stollery of February 18, 1980, and was the Prime Minister aware that the trial date of September 14 next for the hearing of that petition was set, notwithstanding that the first judgment in this matter, which the government lost, was dated May 7 of last year, over a year ago?
What is the explanation for the timing of the Prime Minister's announcement? Why is he following this course within two months of the hearing of that petition? Is it to nullify the court action or to deny the petitioner his day in court? What is the explanation?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: DATE OF HEARING RESPECTING SPADINA ELECTION RESULT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was not aware of that particular date. I was aware of the case which had been taken under the Controverted Elections Act. The House will remember that the basis of the action was because the then Clark government called an election and the electoral officer, under the direction of the order in council, set a specific date for an election. These are actions for which the party opposite was responsible. It is astonishing to me that, having lost not only the general election but the particular election in Spadina, they should be faulting a process of which they were the initiators.
Regardless of that, the object of the action before the courts is to declare the election void, and to create a new election, a byelection. I am saving the hon. members' lawyers money, and
July 3, 1981

the country time, by calling the byelection that they want to obtain. What more could they ask for?

subsubtopic: DATE OF HEARING RESPECTING SPADINA ELECTION RESULT
speechtext: The Prime Minister should get a prize for that one!

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question for the Minister of Transport arises from the critical shortage of air traffic controllers in Canada. Yesterday, in response to a question he indicated that a new training system will produce between 120 and 150 air traffic controllers per year. That will not satisfy the immediate requirement of 250 air traffic controllers in Vancouver, Calgary, Toronto, Montreal and Gander. In view of the fact there is a very major urgency to acquire additional controllers at the present time and, further, that some 1,036 air traffic controllers will be required by the year 1985-86, and under the minister's formula or training program only about half the required controllers will be produced, is the minister reconsidering his plan of action?
In view of the fact that we are now faced with shutdowns at the Calgary International Airport, and perhaps others in the future, is the minister reconsidering his program of action and, if so, when will he be in a position to bring such a program before the House?

subsubtopic: SHORTAGE OF AIR TRAFFIC CONTROLLERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thought I answered the question rather well yesterday. I recognized that there was a problem. The problem is not of the magnitude my hon. friend says it is. I observe that he has bought the CATCA figures as to the number of air controllers that are needed. These figures are not accepted by the department. Apparently they are quite exaggerated. This problem existed when my hon. friend was Minister of Transport. It is not a new problem.
What 1 indicated yesterday was that a number of measures had been taken in terms of methods of recruitment of candidates, in terms of adequacy of personnel and facilities to train
them, and in terms, for example, of developing with the provinces better ways of preparing young people for the job. All kinds of things have been developed to the point that we are now in the position to say that by next year, instead of graduating 50 air controllers a year, the number will be raised to 120 new air traffic controllers.

speechtext: And that is bilingual.

The House resumed, from Thursday, June 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bussieres that Bill C-58, to amend the Canada Elections Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am delighted to have this opportunity to address Bill C-58 which, if passed by this House, will have the effect of reducing the period within which one may campaign for a federal election from approximately 60 days to 47. The bill, while significant in terms of the number of paragraphs, has little consequential effect upon the conduct of elections, save and except for the changes which are necessitated as a consequence of the reduction in the over-all time for the conduct of an election campaign. There are some exceptions, and to those I shall direct my attention later.
1 suppose that the initial reaction of most persons involved in an election campaign, certainly from the standpoint of a candidate, would be to be inclined to approve of the principles involved in the reduction in the period during which an election campaign may be conducted. People in this House very clearly would be most delighted with the general prospect of reducing the time when one is confronted with what may be regarded by some as a somewhat rigorous period in their political careers. This rigorous period, depending on the success of the individual member of this House, repeats itself time and time again.
Canada Elections Act
Upon reflection, however, I think one would also find the general public may become somewhat weary of elections and prefer a shorter period than the one we now have. We have witnessed in the United Kingdom, and in provincial elections, certainly in my own province, an extremely short election term. Parliament is terminated, the election is called and then the legislators are sitting again with a substantial rapidity. All of those considerations tend to induce one, looking objectively at this bill's provisions, to believe that it would be appropriate indeed to pass same. On balance, having regard not to individual ridings but to the nation as a whole, one would be inclined to favour that principle.
There are in mind, Mr. Speaker, two categories of electoral districts that will be substantially affected by the provisions of this bill if passed. One of them is the category my riding finds itself in. The riding of York North is the seventh largest riding in Canada in terms of registered voters. At the time of the last general election there were 80,379 persons entitled to vote. Compare that with the largest riding in Canada, York-Scar-borough, with a total of 108,619 voters. However, between York-Scarborough and York North there were a number of ridings in which the total number of voters did not greatly exceed that of York North. The significance is not so much the numerical superiority over the great majority of ridings in Canada, but the degree of change within my riding compared with the number at the time of the 1979 general election.
In the short nine month period between roughly May of 1979 and February of 1980 there was a population change of
10,000	people in the riding. Yet there had not been the full gap of one year between elections. There were 2,500 people who left the riding, and 7,500 newcomers. The total growth in population was only 5,000, but the total change was 10,000. Given the nature of the riding and its particular circumstances today, I suspect that with the results of last month's census we will find York North's population has grown with a corresponding increase in the number of electors so that it has now in all probability moved up from the seventh position it had in 1980. The effect of these changes, Mr. Speaker, is that it takes a good deal of time to cause the machinery to be put in place which will result in the dispatch of enumerators, the accumulation of information for the preliminary lists and the addition of those who were missed on the preliminary voters' list.
York North covers a geographical area about 25 miles wide and about 12 miles in depth. It consists of three complete towns, Markham, Richmond Hill and Vaughan, each of which is a large geographical area with a centre or group of centres allocated to commercial activities and large surrounding residential areas. By way of illustration, Mr. Speaker, in the town of Vaughan there are housing starts and applications for building permits to a total of 20,000 homes. The effect of this growth on Vaughan will be staggering. Growth in Markham and Richmond Hill is proceeding apace as well. Large industrial corporations have decided to locate there because they have found, as a result of astute municipal administration, the rates of tax there are substantially less than in metropolitan

July 3, 1981
Canada Elections Act
Toronto immediately to the south. This astute municipal planning and prudent tax administration has inevitably led to the location of housing to accommodate the growing commercial and industrial complexes which have established themselves and continue to expand within the region.
It is this growth which will have a substantial effect upon the accumulation of information necessary to prepare the voters' lists properly for the next general election. One can very easily recognize, Mr. Speaker, that there are some ridings, not including mine, that are large in geographical area. We need only examine the riding of the Yukon and the two ridings in the Northwest Territories, indeed the northern regions in all our provinces, to realize the travelling time will be extensive in those areas if indeed members and candidates for Parliament are to be given an opportunity to contact as many of their constituents or intended constituents as they can.
My problem, the problem of ridings which experience large increases in population, is not too dissimilar. While it may take me a shorter period of time to travel from one part of the riding to another, there are more constituents between those two points than there would be in the ridings of the Yukon and Northwest Territories. The problem is the same: time to meet people.
Those sitting in the House, Mr. Speaker, have been blessed by the confidence of electors in one part or another of Canada. I do not know whether it is appropriate for anyone here to believe that he or she is here indefinitely. The democratic process through which we pass contemplates that each of us and those who replace us, since most assuredly we will be replaced at some time, will confront our constituents. Either we will impress upon them our willingness to serve and our genuine desire to benefit the nation or, in the case of an unsuccessful candidate, I suppose he does not meet the general requirements of his constituents.
The process is one of time. We well recognize that, despite the fact we sit here and say that the public knows we serve, there are others wishing to take our place who never become involved in the political process until the date the writ is issued. It is unfortunate but nevertheless a fact of political life.
Is it appropriate, accordingly, for us to take upon ourselves an advantage? Is it appropriate to suggest that the gap in time should be lessened within which we must face our political opponents on the campaign trail, within which we must curtail the number of all-candidates' meetings held throughout our ridings to provide those opponents an opportunity to display to voters their debating skills and knowledge of the subject matter which should concern them in determining how to cast their votes? I should think not. I believe the will of the public is best expressed at the time of an election. Members of the public can best express that will if they are well informed and have an opportunity to see and hear those who wish to represent them in the House of Commons.
We know what happened in the 1980 election. The election was called near the end of December; I recall the House was dissolved on December 14. It was not until after New Years that people began to establish dates for all-candidates' meetings and to begin effectively to engage in an election campaign. We may say that that gap in time would really bring us roughly within the period of time which this bill now contemplates. In the event that we should be confronted with another election at a similar time, we will have lopped off another two weeks within which the public will have an opportunity to view us and our opponents in an election campaign. Is that appropriate? I suggest it is not.
As members of the House we have substantial advantages which are well known to all of us but spoken of rarely. I am speaking of the opportunity we all have to speak in the House, to have our remarks recorded, and to have our speeches in part played back on television. We have an opportunity to dispatch to our constituents householder mailings, to communicate freely with our constituents using our frank. It is an opportunity which our opponents do not have. I am not suggesting for a moment that we be deprived of those advantages, but none of us is here forever. Passage of time, change of political mood, and even the desire among some of us to retire and be replaced by someone in our own party will result in others coming to this place.
It is my submission that it is appropriate to grant to the public the longest reasonable opportunity within which to make an intelligent choice. As I indicated, I have the additional problem within my own riding of knowing that with the massive influx of new voters it will be more difficult than ever to put all those new voters on the preliminary lists and subsequently entitle them all to cast their ballots on election day. From the experience we have personally had in North York, we know there are always complaints after a general election that a number of people have been missed. It occurs as a consequence of the shortness of the time in some cases. It occurs because someone was not home and did not in fact transmit the appropriate information. As a matter of fact, whole streets in North York were missed at the time of the enumeration for the 1979 election. The reduction in the time within which all of this shall take place is, therefore, a matter which concerns me and leads me to conclude that accordingly it is inappropriate to deal with this bill in the fashion which one might at first blush appear to favour.
Let me deal, if I may, with the effects of the reduction in time upon the expense limit with which all of us are familiar. We know that as a consequence of the application of Clauses 4 and 5 which are found on page 3 of the bill, the number of days within which one may prepare the preliminary list and accordingly obtain the necessary information to transmit to candidates for Parliament so that they may prepare their budgets has been reduced from 19 days to 11 days.
The effect on all of us in breaching the expense provisions of the Canada Elections Act can be calamitous. It is well recognized by all hon. members of the House that to exceed those spending limits will result in the loss of a seat properly won,
July 3, 1981

but lost for the failure to comply with the maximum amount of money which may be spent during the course of an election campaign. We also know that those limits vary from riding to riding depending upon the number of electors. It is my considered opinion that what we have in the course of that reduction in time is a risk that we shall hastily prepare budgets which are unrealistic, exceed those budgets, and accordingly find ourselves in a situation where we may have breached the terms of the act itself and placed a successful election in jeopardy.
Clause 5(2) makes provision for the furnishing of copies of preliminary lists to all electors, copies of the pages on which their names appear to identify individual electors with their right to cast ballots. We know that the former practice or the practice which is currently in existence would be eliminated should this bill be passed. It makes provision for the dispatch of a list not only naming the individual elector, but all those electors in his poll. Also the practice of posting preliminary lists in convenient places within the poll region will be eliminated. But the interesting fact is that clause 5(2) makes reference to the furnishing to each person of their name on a preliminary list. One wonders how that furnishing is to be undertaken in the event that we are confronted with a strike of the kind we have now.
I know the practice in the past has been that legislation has been passed precluding the occurrence of a strike in the postal service during the time of an election campaign. Indeed, that might well be the answer. But right now during the course of an election campaign one may go out and examine the list of electors which is posted on telephone poles, where we are accustomed to finding them, to determine whether or not your name has been included. That process would be eliminated if this legislation which is before us were passed.
I say that elimination constitutes a general loss in terms of what the public has come to expect; the loss of finding one's name on the list may result in the ultimate loss of the right to vote at all. The public has become accustomed to a particular way of dealing with elections. They know they can follow a course of conduct which will result in a determination as to whether or not they are on the list when the lists are posted.
I have heard some of the arguments which have been made when this bill was earlier discussed to the effect that the posting of these lists constitutes a danger to people in the community since, in the event that one were criminally inclined, one would be able to identify people who seem to be living alone and therefore set upon them at some time and perpetrate an offence. I do not know that there ever has been any evidence that this is the way in which criminals gain information about who lives where. To my knowledge there is no evidence of there having been a criminal wave during the course of an election campaign, unless we speak of the crimes perpetrated on the public through speeches made by politicians promising things which are never delivered or promises which are changed in the event that the candidate happens to be
Canada Elections Act
successful. It is alarmist to view the posting of these lists as constituting some threat to the community.
I would like to direct the attention of the House to Clause 6 of the bill, which deals with the shortening of the time for the entire election. This would shorten the period of time within which enumerators can be appointed. We are all familiar with the process which occurs after an election is called. A campaign team or a political party swings into action. One of the essential ingredients of a successful campaign is the appointment of enumerators who may, in company with persons from the opposing political party, prepare the list of electors. There is always a great clamouring for extra time so that the lists of enumerators may be prepared.
Over a period of years each political party within a riding accumulates a list of people who can undertake the enumerating tasks. These lists are rather jealously guarded since they consist of the names of people who have proven competent in the past. In the case of my particular riding, and with the growth to which I have made reference and the consequential growth in the number of places or polls where votes may be taken, it has become necessary to continue to update and add to these lists. But the lists are not always perfect and must be checked.
Should an election be called right now, Mr. Speaker, both myself, as one of the persons referred to in the act as having a right to be communicated with by the Chief Electoral Officer in the riding, and the candidate running against me, who at the time of the last election had the next highest number in the vote in terms of his party affiliation, have an equal opportunity to appoint enumerators. At the present time the gap is six days, which will be reduced to five. Members opposite ask what difference a single day can make. I can tell hon. members that it was awkward to put together the lists in six days and now we shall only have five to perform the same task. It is not an easy matter to put together the names of people who are to perform this task without the assistance of the political parties. I know there is a stop-gap arrangement which entitles the Chief Electoral officer in the riding to make those appointments. In my riding, and I suspect in a great many others, the political parties which in the past have supplied this information are generally looked to to provide it again. If I were making any recommendations with respect to an amendment to the Canada Elections Act, I would suggest that this period of time be extended and not, in fact, restricted.
There is a consequential effect of a somewhat similar nature arising out of Clause 11 which would reduce the number of days for the granting of a poll. In a riding which has a somewhat static population it is understood that the polls originally established will not subsequently change in number. In a riding such as North York, which is constantly expanding in terms of the number of electors, one will find the constant need for additional polls. Accordingly, it is of some substantial benefit to us if we know well in advance the number of additional polls which are to be established since with the polls come the lists and with the lists come an opportunity to consult

July 3, 1981
Canada Elections Act
directly with the constituents whose names appear on those lists.
I have dealt with what I consider to be some of the essential ingredients of the bill. My major concern is with the effect the reduction of time will have upon those who have an opportunity to judge the ability and character of those people who are offering themselves for political office. Anything that this House does to reduce that period of necessary exposure would, in my opinion, have a somewhat detrimental effect upon the process with which we are all familiar.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for the opportunity to speak on Bill C-58, to amend the Canada Elections Act. Quite frankly, I rise to speak on this bill because in its earlier forms it was a bill which never particularly concerned me. I must admit that perhaps I had not fully considered the consequence of lowering the number of days which will elapse between the issuance of a writ for an election and the actual polling day itself. But I rise now because I am concerned about many matters with respect to this bill.
I think that we who sit in this House would tend to share the view that we are drifting into something approaching an electoral dictatorship in this country and it is not healthy. It is not healthy for good government that this should be developing. It is certainly not healthy as far as democracy is concerned, because it may well be that that sense of growing indifference of the public to the whole electoral process will heighten. I suggest it will heighten to the degree that we start to minimize the actual election campaign periods themselves.
Let me share a few views with Your Honour and other hon. members of the House. I guess Canada is the largest country in the world geographically which has a democracy. I acknowledge that India has the largest population; but from a geographic standpoint Canada is the largest democratically run country in the world. Surely that should first flag the fact that we perhaps need a longer time-frame than most other countries would feel is necessary for an election, considering the geographical problems we have in this country.
Think of what happened in the last campaign, a campaign which was triggered in mid-December, with a vote on February 18. Think of what happens in such areas as the northern Arctic, Northwest Territories and the Yukon. First, let us not presume that Canada can get by on a comparatively short campaign period. Let us remember the geographic distances in this country.
However, I suggest that a more serious matter is that we are evolving-and this is not unique in Canada-to the point where politics is becoming more and more a media extravaganza. I suggest it is becoming particularly oriented to the 30-second or 60-second clip on TV. Sadly, it is not a question of Parliament itself being exposed so much as the question of the exposure of the leaders of the governing party, the official opposition, and whatever rump groups happen to be in existence at any particular time, such as the NDP at the present time.
What I am saying is that more and more a system seems to be evolving which is not a presidential system such as that found in France and certain other countries, and, in particular the United States of America, but a system which is still the old parliamentary representative government system, one which is treated like a presidential system. The significant item on the national news at night, be it on CTV, Global or the CBC, is not so much what transpired in Parliament, but what glib statement the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made that day, or the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) or the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) as leader of the NDP or as vice-president of Socialist International. In short, more and more people are being asked to focus on the simple question as to whether or not they liked what the Prime Minister said, or what the Leader of the Opposition or the leader of the NDP said. I suggest to Your Honour that that will kill the whole parliamentary system-

Surely, it is strange that we should be standing in this House saying that we should shorten our electoral period from roughly 60 days down to something like 47 days, when our main democratic neighbour, the United States, spends almost a year contemplating prior to the choice of its new leader, the President, every four years. Why do the Americans feel it is necessary to go through their very complicated electoral process of having preliminary skirmishes, of eventually having leaders run to gain the nomination of their respective parties, the republican or democratic party, and then go into the contest itself?

Eventually, that the system evolves to the point where certain candidates are finally put before the country. Even then there is a campaign of several months before the November voting day and a new President is chosen.

Just within the week I saw the outcome of the election in Israel. In Israel there is a minimum time of five months for electoral campaigns. Can anyone in this House say that the electoral result in Israel, which was virtually a dead-heat, would have been the same five months ago? I suggest that the answer is obvious. We found that in Israel, during the five-month or, I guess, almost six-month campaign, a tremendous swing in public attitudes started to take place between
Canada Elections Act
the governing party and the labour party which sought to take over. To me, that is democracy at work. People were given an opportunity to review the positions of the rival parties, to decide during that period which candidate they wished to choose. There was no suggestion of a 47-day guillotine which would have arbitrarily meant they had to vote on what I suggest is largely a question of the leadership charisma aspect that people like to talk about at the present time and which is largely the result of TV handling of politics in this country and others today.
I could take hon. members through many more democratic processes. France has just had an election which had a much longer time-frame than we are contemplating here. France goes through the process of double voting. The first vote simply finds out who the main contenders are and the two then have a run-off vote. I suggest that all these questions should be asked by members of this House before they accept the 47-day provision.
Let me touch now on the question of how arrogant and contentious the government is. This is what makes me so fearful of giving the government another advantage in the mind-bending that it seems to glory in. Just think of the money the government is spending on advertising to try and convince the average Canadian what a good job it is doing. Almost $70 million of taxpayers' money is being spent to condition the Canadian electorate to the notion that the federal government is big brother and is always looking after them. At the bottom line the inference is: "Re-elect us and you will get more of these goodies".
Surely that should cause people to ask if it is wholesome. I suggest that it is not a wholesome thing to have the federal government the number one spender in the country, in terms of dollars, in order to convince people, whose money they have lifted out of their pockets, that they are benefiting from its policies.
If that is put in the context of always getting a little narrower and shorter time frame for an election campaign, then we can see the problem ahead of us. Mr. Speaker, I have won over one member on the government side. At least he applauds when I stand!
Before lunch we were discussing the general proposition of supporting or not supporting Bill C-58, to amend the Canada Elections Act. I believe I pointed out first that I felt we should be hesitant to endorse this type of bill which shortens the length of the campaign period from about 60 days to 46 days. I say that because geographically speaking we are the largest democracy in the world. We have an extremely severe climate, one that is extremely hot in summer and extremely cold in winter. To suggest that we should shorten the campaign period, which at the time of confederation was deemed to be proper at 60 days, to 47 days is something we should not endorse without a full debate.

If we look at other democracies in the world, such as Israel and France, we will Find that in all cases the campaign periods are very long. The only places that have a comparatively short campaign are places with unitary-type governments with a very small geographically concentrated area.
I felt it was important while debating Bill C-58 to point out that I do have a bill on the order paper, C-555, dealing with the publication of the results of opinion polls, in which I have asked that the House consider that opinion polls immediately prior to an election, say for 28 days leading up to the election, should not be allowed in the sense that they are made public,
July 3, 1981

because they in themselves become very unfortunate factors in the election.
I remember in 1980 when I had an opportunity to visit various areas of Canada during that election campaign, and it was very disconcerting when speaking at a gathering at Winnipeg, Calgary, Vancouver or Halifax to find that the main thing the people you were speaking to were concerned about was not necessarily an issue, but whether it was true that the emperor was going to win the 1980 election and get back into power.
My point is that we have to be hesitant in proposing a shorter campaign period so we do not inadvertently give the present government, or any other government in power at the time, an unfair advantage in being re-elected. We all agree that in most instances the timing of an election is up to the government. Very rarely does a government allow its total term to run out before calling an election. As long as the government, through its majority in the House, can keep the confidence of the House it is the government's option as to when it calls an election. To then say we only have 47 days before the actual polling gives members of opposition parties- if they are in the House that is one thing, but most importantly those candiates who are not in the House-a terrible problem getting organized, campaigning and making their views known to the point they obtain the necessary votes to get elected on election day.
I could make various comments on why I feel public opinion polls should be restricted prior to an election. Most of us have witnessed the errors which occur in these polls. It is true to say, I think, that not only are the polls often in error and very misleading, but they concentrate unduly on what I was referring to earlier as the personality cult that seems to be taking over in the political world today. What I was referring to is the fact that it is the leaders that the media seem to concentrate on. For example, in the riding of Sarnia-Lambton, if I may use that as an example, instead of the media concentrating on the candidates running in that riding we often find that the thing the media talks about is who are the leaders of the political parties that happen to have fielded candidates in that riding.

This was discussed earlier during the question period, but during the last election campaign in 1980 the present Chief Electoral Officer, Jean-Marc Hamel, felt he could not hold an election earlier than February 18, say on February 11, because of the time required to carry out a completely new enumeration. Now Senator, that is true. The hon. member for Hamilton Moutain is constantly coming to my assistance and making these points abundantly clear for all hon. members.
The government was faced with a petition which was before the High Court of Justice in Ontario. The first response of the government was to cause the Department of Justice to move on behalf of the respondents-the present Senator Stollery; Mr. Lesley Singer, the returning officer; and Jean-Marc Hamel, the Chief Electoral Officer. The first response of the government was to move to quash the entire petition. The government wanted there to be no question about illegality or irregularity in the election of its favourite son in Spadina, the present Senator Stollery. In that context the government went before Mr. Justice Hughes and, in a 23-page judgment, he found that on all counts the respondents were wrong and dismissed their application to have the petition quashed.
The net effect of that was that a new court had to be constituted-called an elections court-which would consider whether the election in Spadina riding should be declared void. It was structured from an act which was passed many years ago to permit Parliament to deal with this type of issue in an impartial way because, as we know, soon after confederation one case after another was brought into this House. Elections were being disputed for various reasons. At that time it was up to the House of Commons to decide if those who were purporting to sit as members could carry on sitting as members. It was decided that a new act should be passed to allow a court to be properly constituted to decide that type of issue outside the House. That is the process which was in place.
However, by every delaying tactic conceivable the government frustrated the court hearing this matter. Constantly the petitioner said he wanted his day in court. He believed the former member for Spadina was not sitting as a result of a valid election and that his election should have been declared void, but he could not get before the court.
Finally, in May a date was set for the special court to hear the case in Spadina. That date was September 14, 1981. What happened? The Prime Minister-the emperor, as most call him-said he would have no part of that, that he would appoint his favourite son to the Senate, which under the House of Commons Act automatically means that the seat is declared vacant, and that then he would have his assistant, Mr. Coutts, contest the nomination and hopefully win it, and go on to hopefully win the byelection. He showed absolute contempt for the court which has been constituted to hear this matter on September 14 and contempt for this House, which is supposed to have responded to the decision of that court when it arrived at its verdict.
There are two other cases, one in Scarborough Centre and one in Guelph. Exactly the same scenario is in place. At the request of the government in each instance the Department of Justice asked that these cases not be proceeded with until the trial case in Spadina was heard and decided. The government has succeeded to date in frustrating three petitions which were supposed to go forward in order to decide whether three
members in this House were properly elected. We find now that when a date is finally set to decide whether Spandina was a proper election the government has frustrated the matter once again by having that seat declared vacant so that the trial can be avoided. I feel that that type of thing is contemptible.
If can see why the government is so concerned. If it permitted a court to adjudicate in the case of Spadina and it it was found that in fact the election was void, that would mean every member in this House, including the Prime Minister and every member who sits in thb cabinet, is sitting here on a mere technicality. The technicality is that nobody in the respective ridings filed petitions within the time limit to seek court decisions declaring their elections void.

subtopic: TWO-PRICE WHEAT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Bill S-6 is a simple, straightforward bill designed to repeal the Two-Price Wheat Act of 1974 which is no longer necessary as it has been superseded by other programs and domestic arrangements for the pricing of wheat for food. The purpose of the bill is to remove any obligations on the government to make subsidy payments in accordance with the provisions of the Two-Price Wheat Act in light of changes made in the domestic pricing system in December, 1978.
I must underline that since that time the wheat producer has been receiving the equivalent return from the marketplace. So he is not being deprived; the payments are now collected from the marketplace instead of from the government. The new domestic pricing scheme was introduced in 1978 by establishing, through regulations under the Canadian Wheat Board Act, the minimum and maximum price for wheat sold for human consumption in Canada.
To conclude the chronology of events, in May, 1980 Senator Hazen Argue, Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board, announced the range would be a minimum of $5 and a maximum of $7 a bushel for wheat sold for human consumption, with no upper limit for durum wheat. Accordingly, I repeat, wheat producers have not been disadvantaged by the new arrangements and have been receiving prices in line with the international market in view of the higher range announced just over a year ago.
This is where the short version might end, Mr. Speaker, but I see the hon. member for Vegreville has not returned so I will continue to put information on the record for historians of the future who might want to use these notes for learned essays leading to MA and Ph.D degrees.
Let me continue to explain the relationship of the government's domestic wheat pricing program to other grain policies and programs. Canada has for some time had a policy of setting domestic prices for wheat for human consumption in order to provide some stability in prices to both consumers and producers. This is going to be my theme, that these policies protect both producer and consumer. Producers have a right to a fair return for their efforts, while consumers should not have to face rapidly rising costs over a short period of time for a staple food such as bread. These are difficult objectives, the

July 3, 1981
Two-Price Wheat Act
combination of the interests of producer and consumer, to meet when the product you are dealing with is wheat which has experienced volatile pricing movements in recent years due to large changes in supply from year to year in many parts of the world.
I believe we have developed in Canada an enviable package of programs to assist both producers and consumers. This group of programs and policies put in place by the federal government demonstrate a commitment to provide producers with a fair return for their product.
1 think 1 will dispense with the following page or two of my notes because they describe in some detail the existing systems for the protection of wheat producers, namely initial payments, the western grain stabilization program, crop insurance and so on. These programs also assist consumers by helping ensure adequate grain production and, combined with the two-price wheat program, provide important protection to consumers. My notes then go into the usefulness of a maximum and minimum price in looking at the situation as it exists today, and asking the question: Will such protection continue to be necessary?
World demand for grain is expected to be particularly strong during the 1980s. World population and incomes will continue to rise as will the use of grain for food and livestock. The world demand experienced in the last three years exceeded production even though production was at record levels. As we all know, stocks have been reduced. This year the prospects for crops are favourable, both in Canada and elsewhere.
While increased production will undoubtedly occur, it is unlikely that it will increase at the desired rate in all countries or regions of the world, and swings in markets can be expected. My notes make the point that stability will never be completely reached, that present circumstances will lead again to market swings, particularly in prices. In such a market, prices can be expected to fall when production exceeds consumption and stocks build up. Prices could decline to such an extent that producers receive less than a fair price for their product. Although it is difficult to ensure stable prices for grain that is exported-and the Western Grain Stabilization Act helps offset these variations-a fair return can be set by the federal government for sales to the domestic market. A minimum price has been established since 1967 in Canada for wheat sold for domestic human consumption.
On the other hand, when consumption exceeds production stocks are drawn down and prices rise. Recent experience has shown that such price increases can be rapid and rise to relatively high levels. In this situation, consumers are faced with rapidly rising costs. Consequently, it is desirable that the extremes of potential price increases be limited for consumers. Such is currently the case in Canada where a maximum price has existed since the early 1970s for wheat sold for human consumption. The original concept of a two-price system for wheat was implemented in the late 1960s and embodied in legislation for a period of seven years beginning in 1973. On May 26, 1980, Senator Argue announced the policy would be continued for at least another two years.
As was promised during the last election campaign, the federal government is maintaining a minimum-maximum range of prices for Canadian bread and pastry wheats to protect both producers and consumers from wide price fluctuations. Originally, in 1973 the federal government combined the floor price for producers with a consumer subsidy payable when export wheat prices were above $3.25 a bushel. My parliamentary secretary fully explained the details of this program to the House one year ago when Bill S-6 was introduced for second reading. Authority for payments under this program was provided by the Two-Price Wheat Act enacted in July, 1974. A maximum subsidy of $1.75 per bushel was established, which in turn sets the minimum domestic price of $5 a bushel for producers of bread wheat.

In the case of durum wheat, the domestic price was allowed to vary between $3.25 per bushel and $5.75 per bushel. The subsidy was payable between $5.75 and $7.50 per bushel.
Under these subsidy arrangements, the government made payments to the benefit of consumers totalling $396 million between 1973 and 1978. During the period that this policy has been in effect since 1967, the government has made payments to producers of approximately $76 million. There have been periods when consumers were assisting producers, from August 1, 1969 through to 1972, to the extent of some $40 million. The producers have been assisting consumers in various periods from 1973 to date in the amount of approximately $108 million. There is always a discussion on who gets most, the producers or the consumers. I thought it would be useful to put down these figures. Presumably their interpretation can be challenged.
Therefore, it can be seen that the program has provided assistance to consumers and to producers. The total producer benefit up to the end of the last crop year was about $116 million, according to the grain group, and the total cost was about $108 million, with taxpayers being responsible for the majority of the assistance being provided to consumers.
In the fall of 1978, as one of a number of measures designed to restrain expenditures, the government decided to terminate subsidy payments made under the Two-Price Wheat Act of 1974. At the same time, a new domestic pricing scheme was introduced by establishing through regulations under the Canadian Wheat Board Act a minimum price of $4 per bushel and a maximum price of $5 per bushel for wheat sold for human consumption. The minimum price for durum was also raised to $4 per bushel, but the maximum was left at $7.50 per bushel. This action continued to provide a minimum price for the benefit of producers and to protect consumers against wheat prices rising above $5 per bushel or durum prices rising above $7.50 per bushel.
Just over one year ago the government decided to raise these levels to improve returns to wheat producers. As I said before, in May 1980 Senator Argue announced that these ranges would be amended to a maximum of $5 per bushel for wheat for human consumption and a maximum of $7 per bushel with
July 3, 1981

no upper limit for durum wheat. These levels continue in effect today and apart from short periods the market has remained within this band. It is currently at about the middle of the range.
All of this is to say that the purpose of Bill S-6 is to remove any obligation for the government to pay the subsidy in light of changes made in the domestic pricing system in December, 1978. Mr. Speaker, just to set the record straight, I was not under the impression that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) would be closing the debate. As a matter of fact, I think we were all looking forward to his participation in the debate. It was clearly within that understanding. However cognizant we should be of the observation of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), I simply yielded the floor to hear the minister because some of the things I have to say could very well have a direct bearing upon some of the things he has or has not done.
At the outset the minister made two points with which I agree. First, he indicated that the bill has the effect of relieving the government of approximately $200 million worth of liability without the amendment, which really advances the termination date of the two-price system and the obligations provided by the government to July 31, 1980 from November 30, 1978. If this bill were not passed the government would be obligated to pay the difference between $3.25 a bushel and $5 a bushel, which would amount to $1.75, on wheat which was used for domestic human consumption during the period December 1, 1978 to July 31, 1980.

July 3, 1981
Two-Price Wheat Act
The Minister also made another observation with which I agree. I think it should be repeated and re-echoed in this chamber and, indeed, throughout the country. The fact of the matter is that in the over-all scheme of things the two-price wheat system has been a subsidy to the consumer at the expense of the producer, on balance. That should not be forgotten. I am not sure whether that was the real intention of the two-price wheat legislation. I believe there was a disposition at that time on the part of the government to provide for a realistic price range for the production of wheat for domestic human consumption to reflect somewhat a price which would be commensurate with the cost of production. While there was no specific legislative mechanism to provide for a regular adjustment or indexation to reflect increases in the cost of production, I think there was a moral commitment on the part of the then minister, in effect a moral obligation, to adjust that price range on an annual basis which would bear some relationship to the cost of production.
There are several reasons why this bill should not be allowed to pass and I would like to enunciate at least four of them. This bill should not be passed until we receive a clearer commitment from the government, or some direction, on a number of urgent and important policy areas. These are policy areas which require attention now. We in this House are somewhat deprived of an opportunity to deal with questions related to the Canadian Wheat Board and to agriculture.
I know the minister is in a somewhat awkward position, having to answer in the House for the senator in the other place. There is no way he can always be cognizant of what that minister is doing since he is a senator. He does not have the pressures and responsibilities which other ministers have. He travels a great deal and does a lot of spouting off at the mouth. We hear a constant litany of statements which he makes, yet we do not have the opportunity to question him. Thus, we must question the Minister of Transport, who does quite well, by and large. At least he attempts to clarify the questions.
Nevertheless, the fact that this bill has been kicking around the House of Commons since June 6, 1980-and possibly even earlier than that-is an indication that matters with respect to the Canadian Wheat Board and to western agriculture are not much of a priority with this government. As a result, we members who represent ridings in the Canadian Wheat Board area will seize upon the opportunity to raise a number of important issues not only directly related to this bill but also to other agricultural issues.
I wish to place on record four or five major concerns I have with the lack of direction which this government is taking on a number of issues. First of all, there is the two-price wheat system itself. As I said earlier, in my view the government has broken faith with the producers of Canada. I believe it has really violated the intended spirit of the Two-Price Wheat Act.
As the minister confirmed today, it has, in effect, been a subsidy to the consumers at the expense of the producers. There has been a maximum price level locked in under this system for a period of seven years. How many union agents
bargaining on behalf of their union would want to lock in a maximum wage over a period of seven years? It would just not be done. Yet, in effect, that is what was done when the Two-Price Wheat Act came into effect. The maximum level had not been adjusted until the announcement made by the minister in charge of the Wheat Board on May 26, 1980 which took effect on August 1, 1980.
There has been no effective mechanism to provide for an annual increase, both in the minimum and/or maximum levels, to reflect the cost of production, as I mentioned earlier. That is certainly something which should have been included in this legislation. While it was not included there was, indeed, a moral commitment, a suggestion made by the minister at that time, that there would be regular consultation and that those figures would be adjusted on an annual basis to reflect increases in the cost of production.
I would like to turn to the debate which took place on October 29, 1974 as reported at page 865 of Hansard. At that time it was brought out by a certain individual, the hon. member for Vegreville, that:
-we are dealing with a legislative measure which is supposed to give some protection and some stability to the wheat producers of the country, certainly now is the opportune time to build into the legislative mechanism some protective features which would offset the spiralling costs which face the western wheat producers.
We know, for example, that the two-price system which has been in effect for some time now has already cost the producers something in the order of $15 million.
The producers have always been behind in relation to what should be considered a fair return.
If we go back and look at the first four months of the crop year 1979-80 and if we look at the price level on the international markets and the maximum level which was provided under this bill, we will find that producers have provided a subsidy to the extent of about $22 million to $25 million, roughly a million dollars a week. This was done because the maximum price was locked in at the $5 level while international prices were substantially higher. This was really a most unfair situation.
I do not believe that when we accepted the principle of the two-price wheat system we expected a built-in producer subsidy to the consumer for a period of seven years. 1 say to you, Mr. Speaker, that I regret very much the government did not make a retroactive adjustment to reflect the substantial gap which existed between the price level on the international market and the price level being commanded for domestic wheat for human consumption at that time.
When our party was in government we made plans to put in place an adjustment mechanism which would have raised the minimum price to $6 per bushel. That would have had the effect of putting an additional $25 million into the hands of the producers. This government failed to recognize that inequity. Rather, it sat on the situation, did nothing, and in May it made an announcement that it would modify the price range establishing a minimum of $5 and a maximum of $7 per bushel.
July 3, 1981

Since the New Democratic Party and the Liberals combined forces to defeat our government back in December it has cost the wheat producers of Canada approximately $50 million. The maximum price of $5 which was established in 1973 was never adjusted, notwithstanding the fact that international prices were as much as $2 per bushel more on many occasions. The producers have really been taken to the cleaners. We now have another maximum established at $7 with no provision for a regular adjustment.
It is rather interesting to note that in the case of durum, there is no maximum. The sky is the limit. In the case of wheat for domestic human consumption, the red spring wheat, there is a maximum. I suggest to Your Honour that the minister should seriously consider removing that maximum figure, that maximum limit. The minimum price is now set at $5 per bushel. 1 believe that it should be at least $6. Of course, most of my thoughts on this particular bill go back to a year ago because that is when I first wrote some notes. At that time, I thought that $6 would have been a fair and realistic minimum price because it could be substantiated by the fact that there have been increases in the cost of production which could back up that kind of adjustment. For example, if one looks at the increases in the major components for the production of grain from 1973 to last year, it becomes clear, I suggest, that prices would be much higher now. Fertilizer prices were increased by about 115 per cent or 120 per cent. Chemicals increased 168 per cent. In both cases over the past year, I would say there has been another additional increase of perhaps 20 per cent to 25 per cent.
Considering fuel prices, for example, thanks to this government, diesel fuel prices have doubled since this government has taken over office. There has been a doubling of fuel prices. That, too, is a component which must be reflected as a component in the cost of production. If one were to look at $6 as a minimum, one would be looking at increasing that minimum by about 85 per cent over the period since 1974 when it was established at $3.25 per bushel. Therefore, an 85 per cent increase over that period of time is certainly not exorbitant. As a matter of fact, if one looks at the crop production index over the period of 1974 to 1980, one finds it was about 105 per cent. That was the increase in the cost of production for cereal crops. I suggest to Your Honour that there has probably been an additional 20 per cent or 25 per cent increase in that figure over the last year.
We do not have a realistic price range. In my view, we should not have a maximum limit. Of course, we do not have a mechanism for adjusting the price levels to reflect the cost of production. Hence, we are going to continue a situation wherein the producer will be continually subsidizing the consumer. That is really why we find this two-price system unsatisfactory-
The Senator in the other place makes quite a bit of noise about the fact that the Canadian wheat producers have received significantly less than if there had been no price

ceiling. This amounts to a consumer subsidy at the expense of the farmer, Mr. Argue stated. Well, the Senator in the other place is supposed to be acting in the best interests of the producer. I mean, that is his job. We have people here who are ministers of consumer affairs whose responsibility it is to look after the interest of the consumer. However, the basic responsibility of the minister in charge of the Wheat Board is to ensure that the producers of Canada get a fair and equitable return for the production of their grain and for-

I have talked here about the fact that the wheat producers have been denied a fair price for their wheat for domestic human consumption. It is really interesting to note that there are only two commodities which come to my mind that are produced in this country and that command less than the world price. They are both products of western Canada. I am speaking of oil and wheat. Textiles, shoes, and other products on the domestic market command a higher price than in the international market. The same is true with manufactured goods. Why do we have this continual discrimination?
