I am sorry. I did not hear what the hon. member said. However, I am sure that it was intelligent. If it was intelligent, I am sure that he will engage in the debate so that we can hear precisely what he has to say.
The same thing is true with the initial payments. This minister has seen fit to break with tradition and not announce the initial payment level, as has been done previously under a former Liberal minister. As a result, producers were at a loss to know what to plant this spring. They needed some direction. Surely, because the minister is in constant touch with members of the Canadian Wheat Board, he is in a better position to advise what sort of price range will be in effect. But now we do not have a price range established. We can only surmise, from what we read in the press, that the initial prices for wheat and other grain products will be reduced.
Mr. Argue is quoted in the Saskatoon Star Phoenix as saying that for top red spring wheat, the price will range between $4.25 and $5.35 a bushel. That is something which is potentially in the order of $1 per bushel less; yet at the same time the Senator is calling upon the producers of Canada to grow more, at least 10 per cent more, to meet the contractual commitments. At least, if he had given them some idea as to what kinds of grains would be in demand, the producers would have had a better idea as to what to produce for the market demands.
The second reason I believe we should not pass this bill until we get a satisfactory answer is the failure of this government to come up with a clear-cut program to provide for adequate rolling stock. I touched on this yesterday or earlier this week. The fact of the matter is that our grain-carrying fleet is again on the decline. In 1980 we had some 28,400 pieces of rolling stock composed of 14,400 boxcars and 14,000 hopper cars. That fleet is being reduced at the rate of 3,600 units per year. It is primarily a reduction of boxcars owing to their deterioration from long use. The fact is that on the basis of the information which has been provided by both the CNR and the CPR, we note that by 1985 the boxcars will be reduced by about 50 per cent. Instead of having 14,400 boxcars, we will have closer to 7,000.
Clearly, something has to be done. We have to have a clearcut statement of policy about the provision and the replenishment of hopper cars. Everyone who has any knowledge in the grain trade knows that we must have a program of replenishment of the rolling stock. The minister nods his head in the positive. The other day, in response to a question which I posed, he indicated that his studies and his experience suggests that we do not have to order any additional rolling stock at the present time.

The Grain Transportation Authority states that we need 1,300 every year. The Canadian Wheat Board advisory group suggests that we need at least 1,300 every year, and it recommended that the minister act very quickly and, as a matter of fact, pass the resolution. It reads as follows:
That the Advisory Committee to the Canadian Wheat Board urge the Government of Canada through the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board that orders be placed immediately for additional hopper cars in accordance with the requirements recommended by the Grain Transportation Authority.
The authority has recommended the purchase of 1,300 cars each year for the next four years to 1985, and approximately 900 cars per year thereafter to 1990.
There can be no doubt about that. I think they are in a position to know. The Booz-Allen report which was commissioned by the former minister, recommended that at least 1,900 cars be brought into the system annually. That was to include a factor of 15 per cent improved turn-around time. It is clear that the 1,300 cars per year is not unrealistic.
I do not believe that we will export 23 million metric tons of grain this year. At the present time we are running roughly
100,000	metric tons above last year's figure. The latest figures that I have were issued on June 10, 1981 and show our total export of grain at 18,467,000 metric tons, whereas in 1980 the figure was 18,389,000 metric tons. This year 285,000 metric tons of grain less have been moved domestically this year than last year. The total disappearance for last year was 23,882,000 metric tons, while this year it was 23,674,000 metric tons. The figure will not exceed last year's because the fleet is diminishing. Yet we are asking the producers for sufficient quantities of grain to allow us to export 30 million metric tons. It simply will not be done, Mr. Speaker.
The producers will be asked once again to build storage facilities and buy more granaries to store their grain rather than market it. We are slipping behind, and when that happens, farmers lose the incentive to produce.
If our grain transportation system becomes ineffective once again, then our ability to sell abroad will be impaired and our reputation as a reliable supplier will be impaired. This does not augur well for the total grains industry.
A lot of improvement has taken place over the last couple of years and I hope the momentum continues. It is clear that the Canadian Wheat Board can market the grain and it is clear that we can produce the grain, provided there are adequate incentives and assurances that the grain will be moved to domestic and export positions.
The third reason we should not allow the bill to pass, Mr. Speaker, is the continuing and constant threat by the railways that they will ration services in the next two or three years, particularly in the western regions. Yesterday I spoke to officials of the Canadian Wheat Board who suggested that rationing is occurring at the moment. I do not know whether the minister has another opportunity to speak, but if he has, he may want to say something about that. If such is not the case.

July 3, 1981
it would certainly please me very much if he were to set the records straight.
We alE know that this is a bargaining ploy used by the railways in an attempt to get a better rate for the movement of grain. But to hear the minister, the government House leader in the other place and other ministers of the Crown acquiesce and join in the chorus that we are going to have rationing strikes me as being irresponsible. I think that anything that adds to the speculation about rationing is not good for Canadian industry and it is certainly not good from the standpoint of potential customers abroad. To allow that sort of nonsense to be perpetrated, just brings our reputation abroad under question.
I call upon the minister to sit down with the railways in an attempt to work out some kind of proposal to get us off this kick about rationing. We know what the traffic demands are in western Canada. We know that they call for about a 70 per cent increase in the use of rail services in western Canada. We know as well that it will require huge amounts of capital-$14 billion to $15 billion over the next ten years. We know that the capacity is limited at the moment and we also know-the minister will perk up when he hears this-that the railways need more revenue from the movement of grain. It is irresponsible, however, to go out across the country and beat the drums or fan the flames on the subject of rail rationing in the western system. I urge the minister to try to bring the railroads together and to bring the provinces together in some way. This problem will not be solved by one government or one railroad but will require the co-operation and joint support of all components in the grain industry and the industrial face of western Canada.
These are the components of the problem, Mr. Speaker. What we need from the government is a plan of action. This is a national problem and it is urgent. We need answers, not more threats.
I ask the minister and his colleagues to seriously consider the question and tell the House how they are going to deal with it. We need the answers now, not six months or six years hence. If the government is going to allow the railways to continue their campaign of threats unchallenged, then I say it is going to cause a prairie fire which may be very difficult to put out. The railways have a clear responsibility.
The government also has a clear responsibility. It is in charge of putting together a national transportation program and the railways are clearly under its responsibility. It must show leadership and outline how it intends to deal with the problem.
The other day, in his usual flippant manner, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) suggested that if we had not laughed at his concept of double-tracking, everything would be all right. We do not need that sort of double talk of double-tracking from the Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker. It is interesting to note that the minister in charge of the Wheat Board in the other place described the Prime Minister's concept of doubletracking using existing siding, as rather foolish and farfetched.
Two-Price Wheat Act
There is a fourth reason why we should not allow this bill to be passed, Mr. Speaker. I may be transcending the rules of relevance but this is connected to the whole matter of western agriculture and western grain production. I refer to the horrendous mess made of the administration of the herd maintenance assistance program.
I can only say that the manner in which the program was administered reflects the gross incompetence of the people involved. There were several cases where severe drought conditions prevailed and producers kept their herds in good faith. Many spent huge amounts of money on feed. In some cases people qualified, yet their neighbours did not. Certain areas were designated after the original drought area was defined, but upon the designation, the producers found that they could apply for the assistance. Some applications have never been acknowledged and people could not get through to the officials on the telephone. Appeals have not been dealt with and some applications have vanished. There has been no response to petitions, letters and appeals. Three ministers are dealing with the problem, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), the minister in charge of the Wheat Board-not the Minister of Transport-and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. De Bane). It has been a shuffle all around. In Alberta we can only conclude that it is another example of discrimination against the producers in one province. It seems to follow a pattern.
I hope that in his wisdom, the Minister of Transport in his effective way, will ask his colleagues to clean up the mess and get it over with. Some lapsed funds remain and if there is any doubt, the benefits should go to the producer. The government has discretionary powers and I hope that the minister will prevail upon his cabinet colleagues to review the matter and make a decison.
I conclude with one other bone of contention. It is somewhat related to the whole question of western agriculture, namely the payment of compensation arising out of support for the embargo on grain sales to Russia. Here again, the rapeseed producers have been grossly discriminated against because feed grain prices were affected.
The Minister of Agriculture has suggested he will run through the process which was followed in determining how the levels were established and why rapeseed was excluded. But the bulk of the rapeseed producers are in the province of Alberta. I say that if a case can be made for the payment of compensation to corn producers, so too can payments be made to the producers of rapeseed. There is a substitution factor. There is an interrelationship between feed grains and rapeseed meal. There can be no question about that. Prices of rapeseed declined dramatically during that period. Rapeseed producers are suffering. I would hope that as the Minister of Agriculture had a change of heart with respect to payments under the hog subsidy program, he will reconsider and add the rapeseed producers to the list of those eligible for payments of compensation under the embargo program. Then if the minister can convince his colleagues to take action on a number of these

This Act shall be deemed to have come into force on December I, 1978.
When there are three years of retroactivity, there is only one answer, someone has boobed. In effect, we are repealing Section 3. This is a classic example of a serious mistake. I think the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) has indicated in his remarks why the government wants the bill to be retroactive, that is, to get out of its obligations with respect to this mistake which the government made in passing the bill in the House seven years ago.
The major part of my remarks today will not be directed to the current Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin); they will be directed to the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board under whose jurisdiction this particular legislation comes. He is not present in this House, nor can he be, but I know he has a very intelligent staff who will be reading these comments and will pass them on to him.
What we are witnessing today in this request for amendment is a part of a whole series of mistaken and fraudulent legislation put before this House in the last ten or twelve years.
I am not accusing the government of the day or the governments of the last ten or twelve years of being deliberately fraudulent. They have simply made the mistake of listening to advisers who were wrong in 1968, who were wrong in 1945 and who were wrong in 1939. They have been wrong ever since. This fraudulent legislation, by more than a clear coincidence, seems to be funnelled to the farmers of western Canada.
The present Minister of Transport has visited western Canada in connection with a royal commission as well as on other matters. I am positive he is aware that the alienation in western Canada is not just on isolated subjects such as bilingualism, energy policy, the Constitution, and other such issues. The alienation is caused by a long series of the wrong type of help for the western farmer which has only succeeded in cutting his throat systematically and steadily. This legislation is just one small bite at the farmer's backside. That is how he looks on it.
The two-price system for wheat has been talked about for over 50 years. Every political party has talked about it, but not one has brought in a two-price system and presented it to the farmers. Every single party in this House is guilty of luring farmers into believing that they could solve a lot of their problems by giving them equality with people in the rest of the country by giving them an extra price on the small amount of wheat they sold to domestic consumers for human consumption. That fraud has been going on for 50 years. Here we are discussing amendments to free the government from financial responsibility or liability for mistakes it made seven years ago.
The hon. member for Vegreville has dealt with a series of subjects that outline some of the problems related to this bill and related to agriculture in general. I do not agree entirely with his approach to some of these problems. The differences we have are differences that are long standing and sincere in the sense we both know we can be wrong. I do not intend at
July 3, 1981

this time to go into that type of debate. What I want to do is put on the record, as the minister suggested in his opening remarks today, something for the people who read this debate, the historians who are tracking down wheat policy in the west. We must have some form of coherent discussion on the record so they know how this legislation we are dealing with today fits in.
I put the blame on the fact that our government in Canada, as well as governments of other western countries, have been the victims of wrong conclusions by top advisers. This goes back to the fact that after the Hitler war the economic advisers to the government and to large companies, such as grain companies, had a philosophy that there was no future for grain farmers. They pointed to the declining consumption of bread in western Europe, the traditional market for western world grain. They pointed to the deliberate increase in productivity in grain in western Europe and in Russia. They pointed out the growing productivity of the four grain producers of export grain, Australia, Argentina the United States and Canada. On the basis of their study of all the figures they had from the beginning of trade they concluded there would be a downward movement in world trade in grains.
That was the type of advice going to ministers of all western governments. That is the philosophy that still hangs on around this capital city of Canada in the deep, dark corners of economic units of the various departments. The facts over the last 50 years have proved them wrong. Even the politicians in the last three or four years have been saying they are wrong. We still get this philosophy which comes out from the Department of Transport. Civil servants in transport give secret briefings to the research members of all parties of this House on economics, and they are absolutely wrong.
This philosophy comes out in other forms. We hear grain companies making certain statements about how we should do things, for instance in respect of railways. The assumption made by the hon. member for Vegreville that we have to pay the railways a compensatory payment was not the approach suggested by the Hall commission which studied this intensively. The Hall commission recommended the obvious. Since all the indications are that the flood of goods coming out of western Canada in the coming decade and decades to follow will be tremendous. The job is not to cut railways out of existence but to reconsider where the railways should be and what they should carry. In grain alone they have now accepted, not the target of 20 million tonnes a year, but 30 million tonnes a year. In spite of the pessimism of the hon. member for Vegreville, they will attain this target because the railways make money when they are hauling a lot of stuff. The railways make money when they haul a lot of wheat. They make money when they realize that the volume of traffic on a fixed cost industry is what makes the bottom line increase. The railways are still following the advice of economists who believe there is no future for traffic in the west except on the main lines.
Two-Price Wheat Act
Therefore, I suggest to the Minister of Transport that he consider the Hall commission report, chapter 9, where it talks about getting at the problem in an economic way; not loading the taxpayers with costs that are unnecessary. Get the railways off their seats, get them out and get them making money by hauling more than just the few bushels of grain they are pushed to haul under the Railway Act.
When I look at the potash that is badly needed in Europe and the coal that is badly needed in Europe in the next 30 years, I realize it can only come from Alberta and Saskatchewan because we have the Churchill route. I know the United States and Canada have both agreed formally to help Europe out of its problems with regard to coal. The only place they are going to get that coal is from North Dakota, Saskatchewan and Alberta through the use of the Hudson Bay route. The tremendous tonnages of potash and coal required will make the railway lines pay and they will forget all about raising this question about Crow rates.
On this one point of what we are paying as a result of listening to this wrong type of economics, let me say in the first place that this debate was fought out after the Hitler war in the high levels of the department of agriculture in the United States and the reasonably high levels of the Department of Agriculture here in Ottawa. There was pressure put on in both countries, on the secretary of state for agriculture as well as the secretary of the treasury in the United States and in Canada, to realize that farming was a declining industry in western Canada, and that a policy should be followed to reduce production and get farmers off the farms.
This was not mentioned publicly; it was just the type of thing going on between advisers to the government and ministers. The ministers tried their level best to keep that suppressed but, as you probably know, the United States opted for controlling of agriculture. The United States spent huge sums of public money withdrawing good agricultural land, putting it into land banks and grasslands. It ran into tens of millions of acres. The United States paid their farmers for doing this. Our country resisted that. We went the other course of finding new markets for grain. This gave a lift to western agriculture which still exists. That change of direction quieted these experts down for awhile.
The government I am talking about was defeated in 1963 and a new government came in. It was taken over by this economic pressure. As a result, in 1969 and 1970 we had four bills introduced into this legislature aimed at getting rid of farmers all across Canada, not just in the west. They were aimed at getting rid of two out of every three farmers in the west and reducing the land to half, so that the one-third of the farmers left on half of the land that was left in use would make a reasonable living. All that was in the form of legislation brought into this House in 1969-70.
The worst and most notorious of this legislation was the LIFT program. It meant lower inventory for tomorrow; get the farmers out of production, in other words. In this Parliament, to its everlasting shame, that bill was put through. That bill that told farmers "if you do not do what your are told, you will

July 3, 1981
Two-Price Wheat Act
lose your right to sell your product" meant that for the first time in our history a government organization without legal authority directed farmers to get out of producing the only product they knew how to produce, or they would lose the right to sell. That LIFT program was taken up by 87 per cent of the farmers. They went along with it and went out of production. The other 13 per cent who had enough reserves to get through without selling anything that year went ahead and produced. You guessed it; in 1972 the price went up to $5 a bushel, and all these farmers were sitting there with no grain in their granaries because they had been told to get out of production by the same government which sits here now. In all fairness I think every Liberal can understand the feeling of satisfaction the farmers have, because of the type of program they were getting, that a former minister, Otto Lang, is no longer with us. There is tremendous antagonism to a government which would come into a program with force like a socialist state saying, "We have decided we want less production, and out you go".
Then there was a program to get farmers to leave their farms and go into the cities. Government ministers and parliamentary secretaries went up and down the Ottawa Valley telling farmers there was no place for them on farms in the Ottawa Valley. They said that their young daughters and young sons could go to the cities and get jobs. These farmers in the Ottawa Valley are not that stupid. They know what happens to their daughters and sons when they go to evil cities like Ottawa. That meant that the Liberal member for that particular constituency had to leave town. He went off to a safe seat down in Niagara. Knowing all these things, one would think that the Liberal rank and file would begin to put pressure on their front benches and say, "Why are you doing these things to us?"
Time rolls on. As the price went up, as I said, in 1972 to $5 and the farmers got off this low price stuff and began to grow wheat again, sure enough we dropped our long-term agreements with Russia, Czechoslovakia, Poland, Hungary, Yugoslavia and, I believe, Albania and Roumania. We dropped all those long-term agreements for our wheat because, in the reasoning of the government, since there was no market in the future, why get our farmers trying to supply the market? So surpluses built up, and then there was the period of the price wars.
Going back a step, to 1968, the government of the day in Canada agreed with the United States to abandon the international wheat agreement, which was an international cartel composed of both consumers and producers. They decided every three years what the maximum and the ceiling price would be, and they competed between those two prices.
That period of stability for which the farmers had fought so hard ended in 1968, and since that time we have got into situations where price wars have occurred. It was not very pleasant for western farmers to see their Canadian Wheat Board on two separate occasions deliberately drop the price
below the U.S. price in the hope of beating out the Americans. It did not result in that. It did not pay off because there was so much market development and, so much demand developing all over the world that the economists had not even read about it, and all this so-called surplus was soaked up. After the price dipped, it gradually came back again. That is what fooled them on this legislation. They thought that because there was no market for grain in the world because too many farmers were producing, they had to bring in legislation. They would give them a little bit, but not allow them to get anything higher than a certain amount. That is why we heard the minister quote those figures today. The way this act is worked out, up until 1978, if I heard him correctly, there was a subsidy to farmers of about $76 million, but the subsidy to consumers-that is when the farmer was losing out-was $396 million. So what we have is five or six times more subsidy going to consumers, whom the act was not supposed to benefit particularly. The act was supposed to help the farmers and provide that long talked about dream that they would have the same treatment as the manufacturers get here in eastern Canada. They get a higher than world price for domestic consumption, and the farmers thought they were going to get a little bit extra for their wheat. Instead of that, there was a subsidy to the farmers of $76 million, but most of it went to the consumers, or $396 million of it. That is why I call it fraud. To come along here today and say we want to get rid of this legislation and make this act come into effect in 1978 so we will not have to pay any obligations to these producers I think is part of a whole system of fraud.
I am not going to mention the oil fact. I think the hon. member for Vegreville was quite correct when he said that it seems very strange to westerners that even to the extent of breaking the Constitution because of pressure in Ottawa the government has to ask westerners in the oil provinces to take a price less than half the world price. The governments of the west have been fairly generous; they have offered to let us have it for 75 per cent of the world price. But all we can get out of the government here is 40 per cent. This will all change in September. The businessmen of the east have now realize that they are paying a price for not having jobs for their people. As a result, I think we will see a change come this September.
On this question of a two-price system, I think we should call this effort what it really is, namely, a mistaken effort to try to help producers which resulted primarily in a consumer subsidy. Now that it has certain obligations, the government wants to get out of them and add one more black mark to those the government has been collecting over the last 12 years.
I had a list here of all the things which have been done with the legislation over the years, but the minister covered those fairly well. I would like to go on to the principles which I think will be of some use to the government if it decides to continue this type of legislation. At the present time I think the most decent thing it could do would be to drop the legislation, say it made a mistake, pay its obligations and get out of it. However, there is some argument for us to try to keep on and see if we
July 3, 1981

cannot put up some form of two-price wheat legislation which does provide rough equity for the farmer who has to sell nearly all his wheat on the export market so that at least he gets the same smount of protection when he sells in the home market, and I refer to the same amount of protection given to the people in the protected industries here in Ontario and Quebec.
I think that would be a worth-while motive, but this legislation in its present form should not be dropped until the situation has been cleared away and the government has made its intentions clear. It certainly should not drop it until it has paid its obligations.
Getting on to other subjects about which I wanted to speak,
I would like to say just a word about the wider question of western alienation in reference to this bill. I do not hold this against the present Minister of Transport at all. I am aiming my remarks, quite frankly, at the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board in the hope that he will carry out what he has stated his intentions to be, and that is to inform the present cabinet and caucus of the Liberal party about some of the real causes of western alienation and at the same time to put forward positive, constructive proposals.
One of these proposals is to make certain the railways are aware of the recommendations of the Hall commission report. It is very clear to me that the railways are going to pay no attention to those recommendations. They have gone out of their way to try to subvert members of Parliament and the public to the view that they must have an adjustment above the Crowsnest rates for the hauling of grain. The Hall commission report refused to accept that proposal. The railways have to learn to accept it as well. They are not going to get a change in the Crow rates. Furthermore, they should look at the positive proposal in that report, namely to increase their marketing efforts and increase their volume. With a large proportion, 40 per cent, of fixed costs, every time you increase the volume you decrease the unit cost. I would think in a decade they can put those railways into running order, making money, and there will be no more talk about the Crow rates.
This has all happened before. We had a lot of pressure years ago on the Crow rate which culminated in the MacPherson report of 1958 to 1962, I believe. That report took the same position: We will pay your losses, but get out and make money. The push to get rid of the Crow rates suddenly stopped in 1966, because in the period from 1962 to 1965 there was such an increase in tonnage that the railways began to make money. When that happened in 1966, the then minister of transport, Mr. Pickersgill, got up and said never again will the Crow rates come up in this House because the figures show they are making money out of hauling grain. They had doubled their traffic in a short space of time before their costs caught up and they were ahead. I make that point because that is going to happen again. When we start moving our potash and coal out of the west, not to mention lumber, pulp and paper, gravel and other products, the railways will begin to make money, and there is no need for the public Treasury to help profitable companies such as the big railways.
Two-Price Wheat Act
I think that is the first point I would like passed on to the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board. He has to play his part by making certain that under the Canadian Wheat Board Act the railways do co-ordinate with the grain companies and the Wheat Board. He has to know that the railways can make more money out of hauling potash and coal, and he also has to remind them that they have obligations to haul grain under the Railway Act. If you get all those things working and the railways know you are determined to see that they do it, then they will do it. However, they are tough bargainers and this has to be remembered.
My next point is with reference to the Wheat Board. I do not think the Wheat Board can continue unprotected as it is now for much longer. When it was set up in 1935, it was a two-way board. Private marketing was allowed as well as marketing through the Wheat Board. Then in 1939 four pieces of legislation were prepared and introduced in this House to get rid of the Wheat Board. However, they were saved by the fact there was a war on and the civil service here recognized that we have an agency in place to control the price of a major commodity, namely, grain. So the board was saved as a price control mechanism during the war. After the war it was carried on as a price control mechanism until we got rid of the rules and regulations dealing with the special powers during the war.
So the Wheat Board started off as a price control mechanism, but if you read the act, it does not have the powers to control. These powers, which I will not go into in detail, do not exist but the Wheat Board has been allowed to carry on reasonably independently all during these years. There was interference with the Wheat Board by C.D. Howe. When certain grain companies were not selling, he called them in, read them the riot act, and then they would sell a little more. The only other interference until 1963 was by myself, and I explained that to the House, when I asked the Wheat Board to do certain things they were not required to do under the act, and they did that. The Wheat Board was very glad that I did interfere and got them to do things that, in their judgment, they should not have done. It turned out to be very profitable for the farmers and for the reputation of the Wheat Board.
Starting in 1968 we had another kind of interference with the Wheat Board, not reported back to this House, and it slowly lost its independence. The biggest example of that was the LIFT program. No self-respecting head of the board would carry out that program. They knew it was against the law, they had no power to do it, and so the man there resigned and went to a higher place. A new man was put in and the board had to carry out that LIFT program knowing they were doing something wrong and that they had been interfered with. Then as these price wars started, they would receive letters from the minister instructing them to be competitive. They knew what that meant: drop their price, start a price war. We thought we could remedy these sorry occasions of interference by putting in an elected advisory board to replace the old appointed advisory board. All parties in this House supported that initiative. They were supposed to be there to advise the Wheat

July 3, 1981
Business of the House
Board on policy and sales, to put forward ideas to help the marketing of grain.
Now, I want the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board to stand up for these people and give them a chance to offer input and ideas. However, on this particular legislation they were never asked for advice. It is a case of completely ignoring the very people that you set up to advise the Wheat Board. I am not an authority on the legal aspects of this, but I hear that this bill as originally passed by Parliament was changed in 1978 by order in council and the Wheat Board took over the setting of prices. I am not too sure that was a perfectly correct way of doing it. However, I would like to see the advisory group deal with these problems so they can have some input into the Wheat Board. Instead of that, I suspect the Wheat Board is putting a lot of pressure on the advisory board as to how they should think and act.
I could go on for some time on this subject, Mr. Speaker. It used to be that it was talked about in this House a great deal. However, I see it is close to four o'clock, so may I call it four o'clock?

speakeroldname: Mrs. Celine Hervieux-Payette (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General) moved:
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFIT-SHARING BY EMPLOYEES IN BUSINESS
speechtext:
That Bill C-225, to promote profit-sharing by the employees in business, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
She said: Mr. Speaker, it is a great honour for me to launch the debate in second reading of Bill C-225, to promote profitsharing by employees in business. The principle of this bill is very simple. Employees can contribute usefully to the management of corporations and when they do so, we shall all benefit from the ensuing increase in productivity. To this end, the bill promotes participation in management.
For the information of hon. members, I shall give an outline of the main provisions of Bill C-225, which will amend the Canada Business Corporations Act. First it provides, in the case of a corporation with over 100 employees, for a class of shares to be held exclusively by the employees of the corporation. This will make these employees directly interested in the performance of their corporation. A thriving corporation, Mr. Speaker, brings benefits to its employees and to the economy of the country as a whole. Certain members may wonder why this bill covers only corporations with over 100 employees. The reason for this, Mr. Speaker, is that the others already offer some kind of incentive with ownership participation. Indeed, such companies are sometimes established by a group of promoters who each hold a share in the company. However, the attraction of this provision resides mostly in the fact that successful corporations will expand, thrive and eventually have over 100 employees.
I am thinking for instance about Performance Sailcraft Ltd., a company from my own town. Its beginnings were very modest. At first, some encouragement was provided for the employees in the form of profit-sharing agreements. Today, Performance Sailcraft Ltd. enjoys an excellent reputation for its magnificent craft, the Laser, and has several plants and hundreds of employees. This shows the success of this pro-
July 3, 1981

gram. Other members may wonder why this bill provides for a special class of shares for these employees. There are many reasons for this, Mr. Speaker, the first being to provide more stability in the value of these shares, which would be held only by employees and could not be bought or sold for short term speculation. From the point of view of the corporation, this also ensures a stable source of investment capital which would not be subject to the fluctuations of the stock market. The second reason is that these would be preferential or ordinary shares, depending on the formula chosen, with the employees being entitled to receive dividends before they are paid to other shareholders.
That provision gives priority to the employee over the simple shareholder. The employees are the lifeblood of the business and this provision confirms it. Finally, that special class of shares would allow the corporation to pay dividends to its employees by issuing new shares instead of paying out cash. As you can see, Mr. Speaker, the burden of dividend payments becomes that much lighter and the number of shares held by employees that much greater. In these days of high rates of interest, that type of corporate financing which allows the company to retain its profits through the issue of new shares to its employees is by far preferable to any other form of financing, such as the issue of new shares on the general market or borrowing on the money market at extremely high rates of interest.
May I give an example of such a plan, that of The Shawini-gan Engineering Co. Ltd. of Montreal. For a long time its employees have held shares as part of their fringe benefits, which is an excellent incentive since their salaries depend on the company's balance sheet. The performance of the business and what the employee makes are one and the same thing.
Experiments along those lines in the United States and elsewhere reflect the advantages of such agreements. A number of companies have noticed that this measure has cut down the rate of absenteeism. Fewer employees leave their employer which reduces the very costly rate of turnover and the need to find replacements. Waste goes down and the quality of production improves. Better still, new channels of communications are opened because the employees make suggestions on ways to improve working methods. For the Canadian branches of multinational corporations this procedure can also prove to be one way of regaining control over our economy since the employees are the new shareholders of the company.
The second significant feature of Bill C-225, Mr. Speaker, is that it provides for the presence of two employees on the board of directors of the company. That is a new element which derives from the success of Mitbestimmung-that is co-management-in West Germany. Co-management is another way of acknowledging that the employees can do a lot to ensure the efficient operation of the business, confirming their dual role of shareholders and employees, and enabling them to have
Profit-sharing by Employees
their say in decisions which affect them. Besides, having those two employees sit on the board of directors might be a temporary expedient until such time as the employees hold enough shares to elect their own representatives to the board in the same way as the other shareholders. Those managers-employees take some of the mystery out of the corporate operations. It is one way for the employees to keep abreast of its productivity and share in the decision-making process. That is all the more important since the Canadian employees are left out in the cold when decisions are taken thousands of miles away in the international board rooms of some of our major companies. The bill will correct that situation and, I hope, improve the quality of decisions. When someone mentions the presence of employees on the board of directors, we are immediately reminded of the Chrysler Corporation which last year called upon United Auto Workers President, Doug Fraser, to join its board. That was an excellent move which will no doubt benefit this financially troubled car maker. I do regret, however, that the corporation waited until it was in financial straits before making such a good move.
As far as this bill is concerned, I did not specify how the two employee-directors would be appointed nor how the change would take place. I think it is best to leave that up to each individual corporation and its employees. However, corporations could comply with this provision by extending the membership of their board of directors. One of the objectives of this measure is to widen the decision-making base and to this end there is no doubt that an expanded board would be an asset. The choice of employee-directors is also left up to employees and corporations. Periodic elections would, however, ensure their integrity. The only provision dealing with the selection of employee-directors contained in Bill C-225 would allow the board to fill a vacancy by way of an appointment so that its work would not be disturbed by an unexpected vacancy. Some members may also wonder about the unions' role in all this. The first time the Federal Republic of Germany passed legislation on co-management, some observers were concerned that unions would find themselves in conflict of interest situations. These fears were of course unwarranted, as experience has shown. Unions continued to elect their own representatives who are responsible for negotiating salaries and working conditions. Employees elected to the board of directors other representatives responsible for the over-all management of the corporation. Even a thorough search would likely not reveal any conflict of interest.
.The bill will have a positive effect on labour-management relations in that it will lessen the negative aspects of labour relations. Too often, nowadays, unions and corporations find themselves involved in long and bitter strikes, such as the one at United Aircraft in Longueuil, or plant shutdowns. These disputes are costly and leave scars that can take years to heal. Some in fact never heal and the company has to close down leaving its employees out of work. In such cases, everyone

July 3, 1981
Profit-sharing by Employees
loses, the company, the employees and the people in general. This bill will therefore reduce that type of conflicts by promoting team spirit and improving relations with employees.
Why do we need such a bill? Allow me to say a few words about the legislation now in effect and its application to profit-sharing by employees and to point out why it is no longer adequate. Reference is made to profit-sharing plans in sections 144 and 147 of the Income Tax Act. Those sections set forth the various types of plans, but such particulars are unimportant in this short statement. Briefly, employers are authorized to pay part of their profits in profit-sharing plans, their contributions being deductible for income tax purposes. However, Mr. Speaker, this provision applies especially to pension or superannuation funds and is not meant to improve productivity. It is deficient in several respects, Mr. Speaker, and I think the bill I introduced will promote better understanding between employer, and employees rather than encourage savings.
At the present time, profit-sharing schemes do not make it possible for corporations to invest in their own shares. Although theoretically they are allowed to do so, few of them do and as a result investments in a great many profit-sharing schemes are made in other securities. In the case of small businesses, most profit-sharing schemes are substitutes to pension plans. Their main purpose being to provide employees with an income after retirement rather than to increase their profit-sharing. I suggest, therefore, that the time has come for us to re-examine those tax provisions dealing with profit-sharing. I hope other hon. members will introduce amendments to favour a greater share in profit by employees and make it possible for them to acquire shares.
Mr. Speaker, we could put forward many other arguments in favour of this bill, but as we are pressed for time, I should like to hear what other members have to say about this. In conclusion, I should like to add that I have collected much material on profit-sharing schemes in several other countries, which I will gladly share with hon. members when this bill comes before our Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs for a more detailed study.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFIT-SHARING BY EMPLOYEES IN BUSINESS
speechtext:
I am sure they will have something to say about this bill as well, since the purpose of it is important. It is to promote greater participation by corporate employees in the profits and management of corporations. In the participative model which is presented in this bill, and there could be a variety of models, the employees of a corporation with over 100 employees are enabled to acquire shares on the one hand and, on the other, adequate representation for employees on the board of directors would be ensured so that they would have some part in corporate decision-making.
What this bill really says, and what it is saying quite clearly, is that not only do shareholders, the investors in a company, the proprietors so-called, have a share in the prosperity of the company and the work which it might do, but the person who works on the line, in the shop or in the office has exactly the same interest in the maintenance of that company. That does not just include the appropriate membership in a union which may represent the workers at that particular shop, but goes far beyond that. There is a necessity, indeed a requirement, for those people, if they are to realize the full ambit of their work in that organization, to have some say in the direction in which the company may be headed. The workers have a stake in the future of the business and that stake goes beyond just having a job. In effect it means taking part in the decisions which will affect how the job is being done and what effect it will have on the company.
I will not comment on the detail of the bill. That is something which a committee might deal with, if the subject matter ever reaches a committee. If the hon. member's colleagues do not follow their usual practice of talking out their own members' bills-and I hope they will not do that in this case, in fact, I pray they will not-then this matter can go to committee for further study.
As to the special categories of shares, those are matters which can be worked out in the committee. The principle of this bill is clear. If it is passed, then we will have advanced the case against the two solitudes which seem to exist in Canada with respect to the relationship between employers and employees. The parliamentary secretary mentioned a number of unfortunate work stoppages. Over the years it seems we have adopted a confrontational approach which perhaps grew out of necessity-indeed, it did grow out of necessity and neglect on the part of many employers. Both employers and workers have a stake in the future of business. All of them together, and all of us together, have a stake in the future of the country. If we are to advance ourselves in competition with trading nations, then I think we must adopt, or at least look into, some of the commitments which those major factors in Canadian commercial life have heretofore dealt with in solitude. I regret that the Canadian Labour Congress withdrew from the triumvirate arrangements. It may have had reason to but it is still a matter of regret.
If we are to advance in labour, management and ownership, the workers and the government must realize in some way that an element of partnership must exist. This means that one partner must not tread on the other. It is a good thing that we
July 3, 1981

look at this bill. I think we should also look at tax incentives. I happened to have the privilege of being minister of national revenue and I wish to tell the parliamentary secretary that within that department there is the expertise to come up with programs and plans to provide for tax incentives, incentives which would move business in this direction. I think that there is a feeling among Canadian workers that their stake in their jobs is greater than it ever was before. If there is ever an indication of the importance of the worker in corporate decision-making, it is in the presence of the union leader on the board of directors of the company, as the hon. member has said, that company which is having difficulty, and all of us hope that it will survive in the end, but a company which is having difficulty because the industry is having difficulty. I think this is something we should support.
Finally, I would like to say something about a labour-management matter which exists right now involving the Government of Canada and the postal workers. Right now we are moving into a new era. This House and the Senate passed the Post Office Corporation Act. We have moved the postal service of this country from the point of being a service provided by a government department in the traditional sense to becoming a business corporation. It is hiring a manager at a tremendous salary. I think his responsibilities will be in accordance with his salary. At least they ought to be, and if they are not, he ought not to keep his job. If it is to be a corporation, then it ought to run like every other corporation and provide a service. If it is reasonable to ask, as the hon. member has asked, that a firm with 100 or more employees allow the creation of a kind of sharing arrangement in the ownership, and thereby in the fruits of the ownership, then I hope that this debate will not be lost on the government. If we are to have the corporate set-up, if we are to have all the benefits of the labour relations code, I think it is perhaps time that we also have the opportunity to give it to those employees so they can share in the profits of that association. The government, the employees and the people will have some incentive to see that operation work, differently, apparently, than has the department, because that is the reason we are moving. It is to move out of one area which has not proven itself successful, I guess, into something else.
I think that perhaps my friend, the hon. member for Lon-don-Middlesex (Mr. Bloomfield), who is sitting on the backbench smiling at me right now and nodding his head in agreement, should perhaps take the message to the people in the front benches that they ought to consider a plan for that new corporation where the employees would have a stake in the continued operation of that corporation and, therefore, in the service of the country. I do not know how Your Honour translates it, but I think there are a great number of people in this country who would not mind that kind of sharing arrangement if they could see, as a result, the service continue.
As the hon. member pointed out, that is not to say that this would involve in any way a conflict between the employer on the one hand and the employees' union on the other. There is a
Profit-sharing by Employees
great deal to unionism which goes beyond strikes. From time to time unions get a bad name because of strikes. However, there is a great deal which goes beyond strikes. These include conditions of work, hours of work, safety, and a whole host of other things outside the whole question which we always hear about, that management-union relations and strikes are part of the unions' responsibility. The fact that there have been great advances for working men and women in Canada since Confederation, I think, is something that can be laid at the feet of militant unionism.
I came from a small town where they produced-all hon. members have heard of it-Mazola, Crown brand corn starch. It was a plant which operated for years, the Canada Starch Company, under a benevolent owner. People decided to organize that plant. At the time it was organized, they said that would be the end of the plant, they could never make a profit, they would have to close down, they would have to do this, and they would have to do that. They went through all those early traumatic beginnings. Then, United Food Processors came to that plant. As a result, wages increased. Of course they increased, as they would have increased under the benevolent owner, although perhaps not as much. They have had a relatively peaceful history of labour negotiations.
However, from the point of view of the working man and woman in that plant, not only has his or her pay package increased, but working conditions have been better. They never thought they should have showers in a place which was dusty and dirty. Now they have showers. They never thought that there was any safety problem in the machine shops and in the moving parts of the factory. It was brought to attention by the safety people in the union, and a benevolent management recognized that as an oversight and dealt with it. As a result of the marketing stance of that company, the town is prosperous and the business is expanding. It provides employment and excellent working conditions for the people who likely would not have achieved the same conditions but for the existence of the union and the confrontation which took place. They are at this stage now.
I think that one could say of that company, although it is a large one, that perhaps the time has come when a company like that might consider sharing its profit and its management decisions with people who have the greatest stake in the company, the investors themselves. That is the purpose of the bill. I think if it can eliminate the two solitudes or the three solitudes, business, government and labour in this country, then I think the principle is one worth promoting.
In fact, I may say to the hon. member that she is likely on the cutting edge of a change of attitude in Canada with respect to this matter. I commend her for bringing forward the bill. If no one on her side had seconded it, I would have seconded it. I hope that somehow or other her friends will not talk the bill out and that somehow or other at least the subject matter of the bill would get to a committee. As a matter of fact, if I had a motion in my hand, I would propose it myself. If there is an hon. member who would propose that, then I would be pre-

pared to support the reference of the subject matter to a committee.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFIT-SHARING BY EMPLOYEES IN BUSINESS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFIT-SHARING BY EMPLOYEES IN BUSINESS
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, first of all, I want to commend the hon. member for having moved the bill. It is not a novel concept by any means if one looks at world events; but the time has come for this idea in Canada. While I can hardly imagine that by itself it will resolve all the labour problems which creep into society from time to time, I am sure that it will go a long way toward making people feel as if their efforts in the workplace were of some value. All too often, the attitude is that there is management on the one hand and labour on the other, that somehow or other each has a peculiar thing that they can offer and that there is no way that one or the other can infringe on the opposition's area of expertise. I think that is wrong.
I want to say to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General (Mrs. Hervieux-Payette) that I think it is important that we take a look at this matter. I do not want to leave the wrong impression. I do not think that this will be an easy task, by any means. I do not think that moving from the current labour relations attitudes, from the current management prerogatives attitude, to an over-all situation which will embrace the involvement of the so-called workers in the management decisions will come with ease.
I am positive that just as it took a great deal of time and effort to build the labour relations structure which is presently in place-even with all of its faults, it works very well in the main; it works very well in most instances-just as it took a long time to develop the trust and to get people to accept it, it will take a long time for us to get the whole idea of the democratization of the workplace to reach a level of similar acceptance. That should not in any way inhibit us from trying. That should not stop us, as the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) has just said, from having the matter studied further and having recommendations come back to the House of Commons to be dealt with in far more detail.
It is a very complex topic. To support the principle is not necessarily to support all of the detail. The detail does not necessarily always work in the way in which it is conjured up for the purposes of the creation of one bill. But I think that if the government really believes that this is a worthwhile move and that the way to improve the labour relations situation is to involve Canadians in Canadian enterprise, to encourage the commitment of Canadian workers to the companies for which they work and also to Canada as a whole, then the government might look at its own obligation in this regard, and rather than show the way, lead the way.
There is within the civil service, whether it be in the Post Office to which I intend to make reference or in the many Crown corporations which are tied to the government, ample opportunity to enable workers to become involved in management decisions and thus show to private enterprise and the
public that this kind of democratization of the workplace can yield substantial results.
Reference was made earlier to the experience in Germariy of co-determination which has worked reasonably well. Not too long ago I was in Germany and indeed I spent quite a bit of time there some years ago discussing that very matter. I saw how workers can be encouraged and can be elected to management boards.
People on the floor of the shop take part in the decisionmaking. Who knows better about the way the assembly line works than the man or woman whose place is there? Who knows better whether it is being used to its full capacity or if there are ways of improving productivity, of improving safety, of encouraging the worker to share the expertise which can only be gained by pushing the buttons, measuring the stock, taking the finished material and checking it over? Surely that expertise ought to be available to those who may never have worked in the shop but who may have received their education in a university or community college. They are hired to manage but do not know how things really work in the shop from personal knowledge.
I have always felt that if we were to tap the brains of the individuals who make the product and allow them to take part in making decisions about the allocation of resources, the way the line works, hours of work and the assignment of responsibility, then the work place would be more productive and happier. That would make for a better society in general.
It is a shame about a place like Johns-Manville, which comes to mind, where it was well known that working conditions were contributing to the development of lung cancer in workers. The workers knew this but the managers who sat in their air-conditioned offices some distance away from the shop, continued to resist year after year the call to clean the place up and make it safer. In the final analysis, government had to pass a law to protect the workers.
Had the workers been able to participate in management, that need not have had happened. They could have made representations about the benefit that would flow to the corporation if their recommendations were implemented. They would have been more productive and their health and safety would have been protected.
I can think of many, many other examples, where the process proposed by the hon. member for Mercier could be helpful.
For years there has been talk about profit sharing. Perhaps Dominion Foundaries and Steel Limited is the largest profit sharing company in the country. There is no question that the people who work for that company in Hamilton, many of whom are my neighbours, have a great deal of loyalty to it. They may argue from time to time about working conditions, they may feel aggravated or think that they deserve better- that is human nature and I suppose from time to time they are right-but I know from speaking to them that as a result of profit sharing there is far more loyalty to that corporation than there is to others manufacturing similar products.
July 3, 1981

When the workers see production levels and profit margins increase, they feel that it is worthwhile to put more effort into their work. At the end of the year they can see the company-matched profit sharing plan grow by leaps and bounds and know that is is available for them in the future. Such a plan must be implemented willingly, but when it is, the benefit flows not only to the workers in the plant, but to the company and, perhaps more important, to the nation.
1 think that key elements of the industrial strategy about which the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) has been speaking, must be the degree to which we are prepared to allow the people of Canada to participate in decisions about the manufacturing process, and the way in which we harness the resources of this country in the interest of this and future generations.
We are delighted to support this bill and see it sent to committee for study, Mr. Speaker. I should like to ask the sponsor if she would consider saying, when presenting it to cabinet, that if the government were to alter its attitude toward its own employees, involve them in the decision-making processes and show by example that it has faith in its own employees to the extent that it is prepared to invite them to become part of management and if it can show that this results in increased productivity and a better atmosphere in the work place as well as reduced costs, then there might be less difficulty in selling her bill to the private sector.
Someone mentioned the Post Office. What can one say about that, Mr. Speaker? It is hard to believe that a better attitude could not have been developed within the Post Office, and I think the hon. member would agree with that. I cannot imagine that profit sharing would work there, but I think the hon. member could appreciate that if workers had been involved in the management of the postal service and the operation of the Post Office, we might not have a strike today.

speechtext: Are you for or against the bill?

speechtext:
I think you heard me say that I am for it. Sorry, you were not here, but before you came in to the chamber, I said I was for it.
At any rate, in the case of the Post Office, if you were to look at the way in which it has operated, it was bad management decisions which put in those extremely large sorting houses which have mail move from one municipality to another and back simply for that purpose. The people who work for the Post Office, at least those to whom I spoke, said that the system would not work, that it would be less efficient and that it should not be implemented. When they were saying that to me, they were also saying it to their own managers.
Profit-sharing by Employees
They were saying that the system was not a good idea, that it would not work, that the sorting machines, and the way in which this procedure had been separated out from the normal process that used to be there and worked very well, should not be implemented. If this kind of participation had been encouraged by government, and if management had been encouraged to listen to the workers, and if the workers had had their ideas incorporated, I say to the hon. member who smiles that we would not have the mess we have today. Because I happen to believe that is true, I feel it is worthwhile supporting the bill.
It is strange that any time workers are asked to participate in a company, at least in historical terms, it is when a company is in terrible shape. Companies never come forward and ask for participation when things are going reasonably well. They only come forward and ask when things are the pits, when a company is on the downslide and near the bottom. Then companies are eager to have everybody's participation, workers and government alike.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFIT-SHARING BY EMPLOYEES IN BUSINESS
speechtext: That is what we have to make sure does not happen.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFIT-SHARING BY EMPLOYEES IN BUSINESS
speechtext:
I think we have to be cautious. I did not say always, I said almost without exception, and I always leave a little leeway for those unusual circumstances, which the hon. member can no doubt recall, given his vast memory.
That has always happened, in my experience. Doug Fraser was not asked to sit on the board of Chrysler when Chrysler was doing well. In fact, when it was suggested they might be prepared to participate in the days when Chrysler was doing well, they were told to mind their own business. I think we have to try to break that syndrome. That is what this bill does, and that is why it is worthy of support.
In any event, speaking on behalf of most of my colleagues-

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFIT-SHARING BY EMPLOYEES IN BUSINESS
speechtext: All of us.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFIT-SHARING BY EMPLOYEES IN BUSINESS
speechtext:
-here and absent they would be prepared to see the matter discussed further.
I have one last point. It always seems strange to me how companies respond to this kind of thing. When profits are up, companies do not want to share because they need the profit for the future. They say that, after all, they invested their money and are, therefore, entitled to their return. But when profits are down, companies simply lay off workers. It is a strange system under which we operated. In my opinion, a lot of education is required before we will be able to change the minds of the corporate sector. I hope that, with the Liberal and Conservative parties representing primarily the corporate sector, given that they have offered their support to the bill, they will be able to lobby their friends in the corporate boardrooms and encourage them to accept this very enlightened view. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that we will have no difficulty with the very enlightened leaders of the trade unions in getting them to accept that this kind of move is necessary and worthwhile. We will do our job. I wish you well in yours.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gary F. McCauley (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Postmaster General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFIT-SHARING BY EMPLOYEES IN BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) has asked me to speak very briefly, and I will. I just want to reiterate what he has said and what the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) has said.
We are debating what I believe to be a most important issue for the country. My colleague, the hon. member for Montreal-Mercier (Mrs. Hervieux-Payette) has drawn attention to one of the most pressing problems facing Canada today. It is her hope, and for that matter the hope of every responsible member of this House, that we might find some way, some mechanism, for continuing industrial peace in this country.
My colleague has gone further than that. She has stated that the objective of the bill before us now is not only harmonious relations between labour and management across Canada but continued and even increased productivity and profitibility of Canadian corporations from coast to coast.
As is stated in the bill before us, which I will paraphrase, it is recommended that businesses incorporated under the Canada Business Corporations Act create a special class of shares to be held by its employees, that holders of those shares have a prior right to dividend payments, and that employees be represented by two of their number on the board of directors of the corporation. These amendments would apply to all federally incorporated businesses with over 100 employees. I do not think it can be argued that my hon. colleague had anything other than the best interests of the nation in mind when she proposed the amendments to the current legislation. Considering the problems facing us and facing others in the western industrialized world, 1 believe this kind of innovative thinking and fresh approach is needed now and will be needed even more in the future.
If I may, I wish to speak to the two major provisions of my colleague's proposal. Looking first at the question of profit sharing, I agree with my colleague that employee ownership of shares in their own company provides a strong psychological and financial commitment to a particular corporation. I wonder, however, if the British, Scandinavian and French employee profit sharing incentives will, as Professor Ziegal points out, prove to be an exercise in discount buying and short-term profit taking. Studies in those countries have shown an overwhelming tendency on the part of employees to sell their company shares approximately eight months after purchase.
On the other hand, there is significant experience in this country among major corporations in this area. A fairly large number of Canadian-based corporations offer discount share options to their employees and, from all reports, employees are taking advantage of such an investment opportunity. While I am in full agreement with my colleague from Montreal-Mer-cier, there is nothing in the current Canada Business Corporations Act, to prevent employees from investing in their own corporation.
Second, considering the current economic difficulties shared by all western industrialized nations, it could be argued that the proposed amendment to the Canada Business Corporations Act carries with it an implication of compulsion that might prove detrimental to corporate activity and expansion. I want to make it clear that I believe the passage of the profit sharing provisions of the proposed amendment involve not a difference of opinion between myself and my colleague, but rather a difference in the consideration of appropriate timing.
On the whole, I cannot but commend my hon. colleague for her foresight in bringing to the consideration of this chamber such a progressive proposal. I cannot characterize the bill as radical because its inherent logic and inevitability are evident. However, because of the questions I have raised and certain other questions in the minds of some of us, I believe it would be short-changing business and labour in Canada if we as Parliament adopted any measure of this potential magnitude without a complete and fair investigation and debate.
In that connection, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) that the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "That" and substituting the following therefor:
Bill C-225, an Act to promote profit-sharing by employees in business be not now read a second time but that the Order be discharged, the Bill withdrawn and the subject matter thereof referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
